b47b5ba4a3e1c2ba: RAMALLAH: The Palestinian Journalists' Syndicate said that journalists and media workers in the Gaza Strip are facing exceptional and harsh conditions amid the ongoing genocidal war carried out by Israeli occupation forces.

The Syndicate said that journalists and media workers in the Gaza Strip are working in an extremely dangerous environment amid shelling and displacement, deteriorating humanitarian conditions, the collapse of large parts of the healthcare system, and shortages of medicines and medical supplies.

According to Palestinian news agency (WAFA), the syndicate, in a statement issued on Thursday, said that the suffering of journalists is not limited to the risks of being killed or injured while carrying out their work, but also extends to dozens of cases of serious injuries and illnesses requiring surgeries and specialised medical care that is not sufficiently available inside the Strip, noting that 40 journalists in the Strip need medical evacuation and treatment abroad.

It stressed that the issue of sick and injured journalists whose conditions require urgent medical evacuation outside the Gaza Strip has become an urgent humanitarian and human rights issue, particularly in cases involving serious neurological injuries, limb injuries, chronic illnesses, or requiring specialised surgery and rehabilitation.

The syndicate affirmed that continued delays in treatment or denial of access to appropriate medical care could lead to deterioration in the health conditions of the affected journalists and further endanger their lives. — BERNAMA

5d1e170e134b4d65: MADRID: A Real Madrid supporters' group has demanded a public apology from Kylian Mbappe and two team-mates after they declined to fully wear a t-shirt in support of the people of Ceuta.
Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate wore a tribute shirt partially rolled up ahead of Madrid's 3-2 win at Elche on Tuesday in La Liga.

"We are certain that every Real Madrid supporter and every Spaniard is ashamed of the image given by these three individuals," Ultras Sur said in a statement posted on X late on Wednesday, describing their conduct as "unacceptable."

The group, which is often associated with the far right, called for "public apologies" and criticised the silence of Real Madrid president Florentino Perez, with whom it has been at odds since being banned from the Santiago Bernabeu more than a decade ago.
La Liga president Javier Tebas on Wednesday criticised the three Madrid players for not properly wearing the t-shirt, saying "putting it half on is the same as not wearing it."

The rest of the team and Elche players wore the t-shirt, which brandished the words "we are all Ceutans", normally, which was intended to be a message of support for people in the Spanish territory in north Africa, which recently has been affected by a migration crisis.

Residents have complained about migrants from Morocco camping on beaches and sleeping in the streets, with the city overwhelmed amid a humanitarian crisis. Scores of people died while attempting the crossing in July.
The Moroccan Association for Human Rights, a non-governmental group, estimates the death toll to be at least 141.
Mbappe said that he wanted to make a gesture in support of those who had lost their lives.
"The first thing I want to say is that I have complete solidarity with Ceuta and all the victims," he told Spanish daily AS.
"But I also wanted to make a gesture and express my thoughts for all the immigrants who have lost their lives and who are also living in difficult conditions."

Tens of thousands of migrants arrived in Ceuta from Morocco on July 30 and 31. Most of them returned in the hours following their arrival, but several thousand remained in Ceuta, where deteriorating conditions have fuelled tensions with local residents.--AFP
2111c2aec55786e3: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's ringgit and bond market may come under renewed pressure if the US Federal Reserve resumes monetary tightening.
This could fuel capital outflows and complicate Bank Negara Malaysia's interest-rate policy, economists said.

The Fed's 25-basis-point hike on Wednesday - its first in more than three years - has heightened market focus on the scope for further tightening and its potential impact on emerging markets including Malaysia.
The move comes as the Fed seeks to contain persistent inflation, including price pressures stemming from elevated crude oil prices amid the US-Iran conflict.
IPPFA Sdn Bhd director of investment strategy and country economist Mohd Sedek Jantan said the decision's significance extended beyond the rate increase itself.
Tighter US monetary policy could raise funding costs and global market volatility, he added.

"Companies with unhedged US dollar liabilities could also face higher repayment costs in ringgit terms if the US dollar strengthens, while tighter global financial conditions could increase borrowing costs and volatility across equity and bond markets," he told Business Times.
At the broader macroeconomic level, however, Sedek said Malaysia's domestic demand, export capacity and relatively contained inflation provided some buffer against external monetary tightening.

For the ringgit, he said the prospect of further US rate hikes could create short-term depreciation pressure through changes in interest rate differentials, US dollar demand and global risk sentiment.
However, he viewed the pressure as temporary and maintained his forecast for the ringgit to reach RM4.05 against the US dollar by year-end.
Sedek said the ringgit will ultimately be driven by Malaysia's economic fundamentals, exports, commodity prices, the current account and the broader US dollar cycle.

He said some capital could be temporarily reallocated towards US assets following the recent sell-off and repricing of US Treasury yields, but he did not view this as a permanent withdrawal of foreign capital from Malaysia.
Sedek said the Fed's decision did not automatically require Bank Negara to raise its overnight policy rate (OPR).
The central bank will consider domestic inflation, economic activity, employment, financial conditions, credit growth and external developments.
He maintained that Bank Negara would keep the OPR at 2.75 per cent for the remainder of 2026.
He also did not expect another US hike for the rest of the year although he acknowledged that the Fed's projections indicate one further increase remains possible.
Pressure From Twin Rate Risks

SPI Asset Management managing director Stephen Innes said Malaysia could face greater pressure on its bond market and ringgit if the Fed continues to tighten, particularly as the Bank of Japan (BoJ) also normalises monetary policy.
He said Malaysian government bonds were already under pressure, while the yield premium over Japanese government bonds had fallen sharply as the BoJ tightened.
"Malaysia is effectively being squeezed from both sides. US yields are high, Japanese yields are rising, and the relative appeal of Malaysian duration is shrinking," he said.
This could increase the risk of foreign bond outflows and repatriation, particularly among Japanese investors, Innes said.
He said Bank Negara was not automatically forced to raise rates simply to defend the ringgit or bond market, but the cost of keeping policy unchanged was rising.
"If bond outflows accelerate, the ringgit comes under sustained pressure, and that begins feeding imported inflation, then the hurdle for a Bank Negara hike becomes considerably lower," he said.
Innes agreed with market pricing for a Bank Negara hike in the first quarter of 2027, although this could be brought forward depending on how aggressively the BOJ tightens.

If the Fed delivers another rate hike later this year, he said it would widen the policy rate differential, keep US yields attractive and potentially make foreign investors more selective about holding Malaysian bonds.

Another hike could also eventually weigh on Malaysia's external demand if tighter US financial conditions slow consumption and investment, although the country's domestic growth would provide some offset.
Innes said another Fed hike, particularly if accompanied by continued weakness in Malaysian bonds and persistent ringgit pressure, would make a Bank Negara hike a more immediate possibility.
Even if Bank Negara did not raise rates immediately, markets could increasingly price a higher-for-longer domestic rate structure, he said.
Innes said the significance of the latest Fed move was less about the 25 basis point increase itself and more about its implications for further tightening.
"Oil is obviously a major part of the inflation shock, and central banks normally try to look through the first round impact of an energy spike," he said.
"But the Fed is signalling that it is not prepared to look through it if higher energy costs start leaking into inflation expectations, wages and broader prices."
He said the shift in expectations could keep upward pressure on short-term US yields and maintain a firm US dollar backdrop.
Innes added that continued normalisation by the BOJ could contribute to a broader global hawkish repricing, adding to pressure on Malaysian bonds.

17ac1eda8657e07f: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's review of its trade framework with India should focus on removing structural barriers and helping Malaysian companies gain greater access to its market, economists said.
The review should broaden the framework's scope beyond goods to address non-tariff barriers and emerging sectors, they added.

Universiti Teknologi Mara senior lecturer Dr Mohamad Idham Md Razak said the review was timely given the existing trade imbalance and the need to ensure bilateral trade delivered broader benefits for both economies.
"The focus, however, should not simply be on narrowing the deficit as trade balances can also reflect differences in production structures, investment and supply chains," he told Business Times.
Idham said the review should identify why Malaysian companies may not be fully capturing opportunities in the Indian market and address the structural barriers that limit their participation.

"A more diversified export base, stronger business-to-business linkages and greater integration into India's expanding value chains would help make bilateral trade more balanced and sustainable over the longer term," he said.

His comments followed Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani's statement that Malaysia and India were set to review their trade framework over the next three to six months.
Johari said India had stressed the importance of a more balanced trading relationship, noting that Malaysia currently recorded a sizeable trade surplus with India.
In 2025, Malaysia recorded a trade surplus of RM25.37 billion with India, with total bilateral trade reaching RM79.33 billion, down five per cent from RM83.5 billion in 2024.
Malaysia's exports to India rose 0.4 per cent to RM52.35 billion last year, while imports fell 14 per cent to RM26.98 billion.

Universiti Kuala Lumpur Business School economic analyst Associate Professor Dr Aimi Zulhazmi Abdul Rashid said the review of the Malaysia-India Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (MICECA) was apt given changes in the countries' trade and investment landscape since the deal was signed in 2011.

Aimi said the agreement needed to evolve beyond its traditional focus on goods to address non-tariff barriers, rules of origin and emerging areas such as digital trade, semiconductors, fintech and renewable energy.
"The 2011 agreement is goods-heavy. A 2026 review must be services and value-chain heavy," he added.

Idham said the review should look closely at tariff lines where Malaysian products still faced relatively high duties. This is alongside rules of origin, customs procedures and non-tariff measures such as product standards, certification and licensing requirements.

He also said there was scope to strengthen provisions covering services, digital trade and investment, while improving trade facilitation through greater use of digital customs and regulatory cooperation.
"The objective should be to make the agreement more responsive to today's business environment and reduce the practical cost of entering the Indian market," he said.
Aimi similarly highlighted rules of origin and non-tariff barriers as key areas for review, particularly for Malaysia's electrical and electronics and semiconductor industries.
"Current AITIGA uses uniform 35 per cent local value addition. This hurts electronics and semiconductors where value addition is low but supply chains are global.
"India and Malaysia are already discussing Product Specific Rules (PSR) to give flexibility. This is critical for Malaysia's E&E exports," he said.
On sectors with potential for greater Malaysian participation in India, Idham said Malaysia already possessed established industrial and technological capabilities in certain sectors.
They include electrical and electronics, semiconductors and related components, chemicals, palm oil and downstream palm-based products, processed food and halal products.
"There is also potential in healthcare, digital services, renewable energy and other green technologies as India's economy continues to expand," he said.

He said Malaysian companies should pursue higher-value segments and strengthen their distribution networks, partnerships and joint ventures in India rather than focusing solely on increasing export volumes.
"This would allow Malaysian companies to build a more durable presence in one of the world's largest consumer and industrial markets," he said.
Meanwhile, Aimi said Malaysia should likewise use India's vast consumer market to expand trade in both directions.
"Given India's 1.4 billion consumer market, Malaysia should not compete on low-cost mass manufacturing, but on 3 layers," he said.

Aimi identified palm oil and oleochemicals, E&E and machinery as areas where Malaysia could strengthen existing trade, while also expanding into halal products, chemicals, green energy, medical devices and high-value agri-food.
He also pointed to services including healthcare, education, fintech, Islamic finance, construction and engineering as areas where Malaysia was under-exported.

6e32e76c95e0e40f: A newsroom can spend an entire day reporting arguments and still fail to show how people live with one another.
That is an uncomfortable thought at a time when race and religion can turn an ordinary disagreement into a national argument within hours.
The loudest voices travel fastest. A provocative remark sparks a counterattack, which invites another, until the original issue is almost beside the point.
It was against this backdrop that FMT executive chairman Nelson Fernandez spoke about the role of newsrooms in reporting race and religion at the New Muslim Community Conference.
His argument was not that journalism should avoid difficult stories or seek some moral high ground.
It was more demanding than that. Report the difficult truth, but do not allow the difficulty to become the whole story.
“Conflict is part of news. It should not become the only news,” he said.
Journalism has always been drawn to conflict because it carries drama, consequence and urgency.
Digital media has intensified that instinct. Outrage is immediate, measurable and endlessly renewable.

A story can still be undergoing verification in a newsroom while another version is already circulating online, attracting comments and being turned into ammunition by people who may never have read the original report.
The temptation is obvious: stay in the argument because that is where the audience is.
But journalism also has to decide what happens next. Do we find another angry voice and keep the argument alive?
Or do we establish what happened, add the missing context, test the claims and find the information that allows people to understand the issue rather than simply react to it?
That is not uniquely Malaysian. Mature media systems have wrestled with the same tension between the public’s right to know and the potential harm caused by careless or distorted reporting.
The US Society of Professional Journalists places seeking truth alongside minimising harm, calling for verification, context, responses to allegations, avoidance of stereotyping and corrections.

Australia's Press Council similarly says references to race, ethnicity and nationality should be relevant and in the public interest, warning against allowing an individual’s actions to become a judgment on an entire community.
Britain's Ofcom, meanwhile, makes clear that due impartiality does not mean giving every argument equal weight; it means giving appropriate weight according to evidence and context.
There is a useful lesson here for Malaysia.
Before putting race or religion into a headline, a newsroom should be able to answer a simple question: why does it belong there?
Not whether somebody might be offended. Not whether it will generate clicks. But whether it is relevant, accurate and necessary to understanding what happened.
That distinction also protects journalism from confusing fairness with false equivalence.
If an allegation is unsupported and the evidence points elsewhere, giving both positions equal prominence does not make the report more balanced.
Scrutiny without collective blame

A newsroom should be able to scrutinise government policy, a religious institution, a political party or a powerful individual without turning that scrutiny into an attack on everyone who shares an identity with the subject.

FMT’s reporting on Tabung Haji illustrates the point. Religious significance cannot place an institution beyond legitimate questioning, but scrutiny of an establishment must not become shorthand for hostility towards the faith associated with it.
Challenge the institution, establish the facts and question the conduct without making a community answer for it.

This is also where Saifuddin Abdullah’s response to Fernandez adds something useful. The Indera Mahkota MP argued that Malaysians should move beyond merely tolerating differences towards understanding and celebrating them.
That may sound like a small distinction, but it goes to the heart of the discussion.
Tolerance can mean learning to live with people we do not understand. Respect requires us to make the effort to understand them.
Journalism cannot be expected to celebrate every difference, but it can help prevent difference from becoming caricature.
And that begins in the newsroom.
Fernandez's point about a multiracial workforce is not simply that different people should occupy the same office.

Its real value lies in what happens before publication: one journalist notices a cultural sensitivity another has missed; a colleague questions a headline; someone checks whether a translation has altered the meaning; another asks whether an individual’s conduct could wrongly be read as a judgment on an entire community.
That is diversity doing editorial work.
It creates the possibility of challenge without hostility, and of disagreement without division.
The value of being trusted
The wider media environment makes this more important.

The 2026 Reuters Institute Digital News Report found that social and video platforms have become major gateways to news, with 27% of respondents globally saying they get news from individual creators or influencers.
Yet such creators are generally regarded as less trustworthy and less impartial than traditional news sources, while overall trust in news has fallen to 37%.
When everyone can publish, journalism’s scarce commodity is no longer access to a platform.
It is credibility.
That becomes even more important when artificial intelligence can produce convincing images, audio and video.
The Society of Professional Journalists is now proposing a major revision of its ethics code, strengthening guidance on verification, misinformation and AI-generated material.
The future may therefore belong less to the organisation that is first to tell us something happened than to the one people trust to tell them what actually happened.
And that brings us to a little girl.
A lesson in unity
The story of Diya Amanda is powerful not because it offers a convenient lesson in unity, but because it revealed something the outrage economy rarely captures.
A Chinese woman came to the newsroom seeking help. An Indian journalist told the story. A Malay child needed treatment. Malaysians from different communities responded.
The newsroom did not ask readers to put aside their racial identities. It did not manufacture a moment of national harmony.
It made a human need visible. People responded to it.
That may be the most important point in Fernandez’s speech.
Malaysia does not need journalism to manufacture unity. Much of the time, the evidence of our ability to care for one another is already there.
What journalism chooses to make visible can determine whether we see it.
Conflict will always be news. So will wrongdoing, hypocrisy, prejudice and failure. A responsible newsroom cannot turn away from those things because they are uncomfortable.
But neither should it allow the most divisive voices to become the default description of the country.
There is a Malaysia that shouts, and there is also a Malaysia that helps.
One trends, the other often does not.
Perhaps the task of journalism is not to make people feel better about their country. It is to make sure they see enough of it to understand it honestly.

That means reporting the argument without becoming part of the argument; scrutiny without stereotyping; fairness without false equivalence; compassion without sentimentality; and corrections without defensiveness.
Above all, it means remembering that the country exists beyond its loudest headlines.
The Malaysia our headlines rarely show may be the one worth looking for.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
428f1da31778f480: Sebuah bilik berita boleh menghabiskan sepanjang hari melaporkan pertelingkahan, tetapi masih gagal menunjukkan bagaimana rakyat sebenarnya hidup bersama.
Itulah hakikat yang kurang selesa pada ketika isu kaum dan agama boleh mengubah perselisihan biasa menjadi polemik nasional dalam tempoh beberapa jam.
Suara paling lantang biasanya paling cepat tersebar. Satu kenyataan provokatif mencetuskan serangan balas, kemudian dibalas lagi, sehingga isu asal hampir tenggelam.
Dalam suasana inilah Pengerusi Eksekutif FMT Nelson Fernandez bercakap mengenai peranan bilik berita dalam melaporkan isu kaum dan agama pada New Muslim Community Conference.
Hujahnya bukan supaya wartawan mengelak isu sukar atau cuba meletakkan diri pada kedudukan moral yang lebih tinggi.
Tuntutannya sebenarnya lebih besar: laporkan kebenaran yang sukar, tetapi jangan biarkan konflik itu menjadi satu-satunya gambaran sesuatu isu.
“Konflik adalah sebahagian daripada berita. Tetapi ia tidak sepatutnya menjadi satu-satunya berita,” katanya.
Kewartawanan sememangnya tertarik kepada konflik kerana ia mempunyai unsur drama, kesan dan kepentingan segera.
Media digital menguatkan lagi kecenderungan itu. Kemarahan boleh tercetus serta-merta, diukur melalui angka dan terus dipanjangkan.

Ketika sesebuah berita masih melalui proses pengesahan di bilik berita, versi lain mungkin sudah tersebar dalam talian, menerima komen dan dijadikan bahan serangan oleh mereka yang mungkin langsung tidak membaca laporan asal.
Godaan untuk terus berada dalam pertelingkahan itu memang besar kerana di situlah perhatian khalayak tertumpu.
Namun kewartawanan juga perlu menentukan apa yang harus berlaku selepas itu. Adakah kita mencari satu lagi suara marah untuk terus memanjangkan pertelingkahan?
Atau kita menentukan apa sebenarnya berlaku, memberikan konteks yang hilang, menguji dakwaan dan mencari maklumat yang membantu orang ramai memahami isu, bukan sekadar bertindak balas terhadapnya?
Dilema ini bukan unik kepada Malaysia. Sistem media yang matang juga berdepan ketegangan antara hak masyarakat untuk mengetahui dan risiko kemudaratan akibat laporan yang cuai atau terpesong.

Society of Professional Journalists di Amerika Syarikat meletakkan usaha mencari kebenaran seiring dengan tanggungjawab meminimumkan kemudaratan, termasuk melalui pengesahan fakta, konteks, hak menjawab tuduhan, mengelakkan stereotaip dan membuat pembetulan.

Australian Press Council pula menetapkan bahawa rujukan kepada kaum, etnik dan kewarganegaraan perlu relevan serta mempunyai kepentingan awam. Tindakan seseorang juga tidak sepatutnya dijadikan asas untuk menghukum seluruh komunitinya.

Ofcom di United Kingdom pula menjelaskan bahawa sikap berkecuali tidak bermaksud setiap hujah mesti diberikan ruang sama rata. Sebaliknya, ruang perlu diberikan secara wajar berdasarkan bukti dan konteks.
Ada pengajaran berguna untuk Malaysia.
Sebelum kaum atau agama dimasukkan dalam tajuk berita, sesebuah bilik berita perlu dapat menjawab satu soalan mudah: mengapa perkara itu perlu disebut?
Bukan sama ada seseorang mungkin tersinggung. Bukan sama ada ia mampu menarik klik. Tetapi sama ada perkara itu relevan, tepat dan penting untuk memahami apa sebenarnya berlaku.
Perbezaan itu juga penting supaya kewartawanan tidak menyamakan keadilan dengan memberikan ruang sama rata kepada dakwaan yang tidak setara.
Jika sesuatu dakwaan tidak mempunyai asas dan bukti menunjukkan sebaliknya, memberikan penonjolan sama kepada kedua-dua pihak tidak semestinya menjadikan laporan lebih seimbang.
Tegas tanpa menyalahkan seluruh komuniti

Bilik berita seharusnya boleh meneliti dasar kerajaan, institusi agama, parti politik atau individu berpengaruh tanpa menjadikan penelitian itu sebagai serangan terhadap semua orang yang berkongsi identiti dengan pihak berkenaan.

Liputan FMT mengenai Tabung Haji menunjukkan perkara itu. Kepentingan agamanya tidak bermaksud institusi berkenaan tidak boleh dipersoalkan, tetapi penelitian terhadap sesebuah institusi juga tidak boleh disamakan dengan permusuhan terhadap agama yang dikaitkan dengannya.
Persoalkan institusi, tentukan fakta dan teliti tindakannya tanpa menjadikan seluruh komuniti bertanggungjawab.
Di sinilah pandangan Ahli Parlimen Indera Mahkota Saifuddin Abdullah terhadap ucapan Fernandez turut memberi perspektif berguna.
Saifuddin berhujah bahawa rakyat Malaysia perlu melangkaui sekadar bertoleransi terhadap perbezaan, kepada usaha memahami dan meraikannya.
Perbezaannya mungkin kelihatan kecil, tetapi itulah inti pati perbincangan ini.
Toleransi boleh bermaksud kita belajar hidup bersama orang yang tidak kita fahami. Rasa hormat pula memerlukan kita berusaha memahami mereka.
Kewartawanan tidak perlu meraikan setiap perbezaan, tetapi ia boleh membantu memastikan perbezaan tidak berubah menjadi gambaran stereotaip.
Dan usaha itu bermula di bilik berita.
Pandangan Fernandez mengenai tenaga kerja berbilang kaum bukan sekadar bermaksud individu daripada latar belakang berbeza bekerja di pejabat yang sama.

Nilai sebenar kepelbagaian itu dapat dilihat sebelum sesuatu laporan diterbitkan: seorang wartawan menyedari sensitiviti budaya yang terlepas pandang oleh rakannya; seorang lagi mempersoalkan tajuk berita; ada yang memastikan terjemahan tidak mengubah maksud; dan yang lain bertanya sama ada tindakan seseorang boleh disalah anggap sebagai gambaran seluruh komunitinya.
Itulah kepelbagaian yang memainkan peranan dalam proses editorial.
Ia membuka ruang untuk saling mencabar pandangan tanpa bermusuhan, dan berbeza pendapat tanpa mencetuskan perpecahan.
Nilai sebuah kepercayaan
Persekitaran media hari ini menjadikan perkara itu semakin penting.

Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026 mendapati platform sosial dan video semakin menjadi pintu utama mendapatkan berita, dengan 27% responden di seluruh dunia mendapatkan berita daripada pencipta kandungan atau pempengaruh individu.

Namun golongan itu secara umumnya dianggap kurang boleh dipercayai dan kurang berkecuali berbanding sumber berita tradisional, manakala tahap kepercayaan keseluruhan terhadap berita merosot kepada 37%.
Apabila semua orang boleh menerbitkan sesuatu, perkara paling berharga dalam kewartawanan bukan lagi akses kepada platform.
Sebaliknya, ia adalah kredibiliti.
Hal itu menjadi semakin penting apabila kecerdasan buatan mampu menghasilkan gambar, audio dan video yang meyakinkan.
Society of Professional Journalists kini mencadangkan rombakan besar terhadap kod etikanya dengan memperkukuh panduan mengenai pengesahan, maklumat palsu dan bahan dijana AI.
Masa depan mungkin bukan milik organisasi yang paling cepat memberitahu kita sesuatu telah berlaku, tetapi organisasi yang paling dipercayai untuk memberitahu apa sebenarnya yang berlaku.
Dan di sinilah kisah seorang kanak-kanak perempuan menjadi penting.
Pengajaran mengenai perpaduan
Kisah Diya Amanda berkesan bukan kerana ia menawarkan mesej perpaduan yang mudah, tetapi kerana ia menunjukkan sesuatu yang jarang mendapat perhatian dalam dunia media yang dipacu kemarahan.

Seorang wanita Cina datang ke bilik berita meminta bantuan. Seorang wartawan India menceritakan kisahnya. Seorang kanak-kanak Melayu memerlukan rawatan. Rakyat Malaysia daripada pelbagai kaum tampil membantu.
Bilik berita tidak meminta pembaca mengetepikan identiti kaum mereka. Ia juga tidak mereka-reka suatu detik keharmonian nasional.
Ia hanya mengetengahkan keperluan seorang manusia. Orang ramai kemudian tampil membantu.
Itulah mungkin mesej paling penting dalam ucapan Fernandez.
Malaysia tidak memerlukan kewartawanan untuk mencipta perpaduan. Dalam banyak keadaan, bukti bahawa rakyat mampu saling mengambil berat sebenarnya sudah pun wujud.
Apa yang dipilih oleh kewartawanan untuk diketengahkan boleh menentukan sama ada kita melihatnya atau tidak.

Konflik akan sentiasa menjadi berita. Begitu juga salah laku, kemunafikan, prejudis dan kegagalan. Bilik berita yang bertanggungjawab tidak boleh berpaling daripada perkara itu hanya kerana ia tidak menyenangkan.
Namun media juga tidak sepatutnya membiarkan suara paling memecahbelahkan menjadi gambaran utama negara ini.
Ada Malaysia yang lantang bertengkar, dan ada juga Malaysia yang sentiasa menghulurkan bantuan.
Yang pertama mudah menjadi tular. Yang kedua sering tidak mendapat perhatian.

Mungkin tugas kewartawanan bukan untuk membuat rakyat berasa lebih baik mengenai negara mereka. Sebaliknya, tugasnya memastikan rakyat melihat gambaran yang cukup luas untuk memahami negara ini dengan jujur.

Ini bermaksud melaporkan pertelingkahan tanpa menjadi sebahagian daripadanya; melakukan penelitian tanpa stereotaip; berlaku adil tanpa menyamakan perkara yang tidak setara; menunjukkan belas ihsan tanpa berlebihan; dan membuat pembetulan tanpa bersikap defensif.
Paling penting, kita perlu ingat bahawa Malaysia lebih luas daripada tajuk berita yang paling lantang.
Malaysia yang jarang muncul dalam tajuk berita kita mungkin sebenarnya Malaysia yang patut kita beri perhatian.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
1acc4ac3da8d662d: GUA MUSANG: Lipstick, eyeliner and face powder may seem far removed from the forest, but for women in the Temiar community in this part of Kelantan, they are helping keep an old beauty tradition alive.
Facial art featuring long lines, waves and dots has been passed down through generations, with each motif carrying its own meaning.
Traditionally, the colours came from natural materials such as charcoal, limestone paste and kesumba seeds. Today, however, some of those ingredients are becoming harder to find.
Endah Angah, 37, told Bernama that modern cosmetics offer a practical alternative, particularly when gathering traditional materials means venturing deeper into the forest.
“In the past, obtaining these natural ingredients was easy, so we didn’t have to go deep into the forest to look for them,” she explained. “But now, they’re getting harder to find.”
Lipstick and eyeliner can also produce brighter, neater patterns that last longer on the skin, she added.

For her and others in the community, changing the materials does not mean changing tradition itself. Rahimah Punai, 39, said every line and dot is still drawn carefully because the designs carry meanings inherited from their ancestors.
“The lines represent the river, while the dots symbolise our connection to nature,” she said, stressing that the patterns are not simply decorative and cannot be altered according to personal taste.
“We have to follow what our ancestors passed down to us and keep it the same to preserve our customs and heritage. We cannot just add streaks to the forehead, nose or cheeks.”
The facial art continues to be worn during occasions such as Sewang (traditional dance) ceremonies and community gatherings, keeping it visible in everyday cultural life.
Abong Busu, 55, said such events also provide an opportunity for younger members of the community to learn what the designs mean, rather than simply copy how they look.
“This is how we introduce the tradition to the younger generation,” she said. “The children are very interested and often ask us a lot of questions about it.”
This matters because the practice is carried not only through the finished designs, but through the stories and explanations shared while they are being applied.
Kelantan culture and arts department director Rohaniza Abdullah said the use of modern cosmetics shows how the tradition can adapt while retaining original motifs and colours.

Of course, for the women who continue to wear the designs, that balance is already familiar. The tools may be newer and easier to find, but the meaning behind every line and dot remains: tied to the same rivers, forests and ancestral knowledge that shaped the tradition to begin with.

4a5259579095bd8f: TEL AVIV: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu kicked off his Likud party's election campaign on Thursday with a speech focussed on security concerns.

Netanyahu has come under fire for his government's failure to prevent the Hamas-led Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel, the deadliest in the country's history, but on Thursday he insisted that he and his party "are the only ones who can guarantee Israel's security".

He went on to list Israeli military operations that have taken place in Iran, Lebanon, Syria and the Gaza Strip since 2023. "The mission must be completed, we must bring down the Iranian regime and totally destroy Hezbollah and Hamas," he said.
He also accused his rivals of wanting to make "territorial concessions", and pointed to Israeli troops in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza as evidence that "we take land instead of giving it".
The premier repeated his refrain that he "has changed the face of the Middle East", vowing to change it yet again, without offering specifics.

Netanyahu heads the most right-wing government in Israeli history. He has led his country into a series of wars while ramping up construction of settlements - deemed illegal under international law - in the occupied West Bank, where violence has surged since the Gaza war began.
He is the first head of government to face a criminal trial, with several corruption charges levelled against him, which he denies.

Opinion polls show the Oct 27 elections are likely to be close. The bloc led by Netanyahu and his far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies are squaring off against that of his main opponent, centrist Gadi Eisenkot, who is backed by parties from both the right and the left.
f6e00a0870b35044: Manchester United are finding new ways to make the wrong kind of history.
The loss to Brighton was the first time in 50 years that a two-goal lead at Old Trafford has been turned into a defeat.
“Two-nil up and you messed it up,” was the printable version of what the visiting fans sang.
There were unavoidable echoes of last year’s loss at Grimsby as the Carabao Cup again proved a poisoned chalice.
Then it was on penalties to a fourth-tier side in the second round; this year it was a third-round home tie against a Premier League club, but one with something of a hex over them.
The Seagulls had won on four of their five previous visits.
The shock was much lower on the Richter Scale, but it’s still Brighton, regarded by many as a feeder club!
But what feeds the knockers and fuels the narrative that United could be teetering into crisis territory isn’t one single misstep.
Michael Carrick himself acknowledged that “a couple of smaller things ended up accumulating into something bigger.”
Honest as ever, he refused to blame bad luck, but it’s played a significant part in tandem with “Sod’s Law”.
Top of the list has to be Erling Haaland’s now-infamous “offside goal” in the derby. An apology from Pro Ref (the referee’s body) only rubbed salt into that wound.
And forgotten in the furore is that United almost snatched a draw at the death, being denied only by an amazing point-blank save from Gianluigi Donnarumma.
But few of their own fans would argue that United deserved anything other than a defeat after playing second fiddle to 10 men for over 70 minutes.
The “couple” of things would no doubt also include Everton’s last-minute equaliser – a once-in-a-career thunderbolt from Ainsley Maitland-Niles, of all people, the previous weekend.
Another would be the fan revolt over the club’s ticketing crackdown. This led to a single banner inside the ground, displaying the words, "The way you treat us is a disgrace."
Another apology, from the club this time, but nothing can restore the faith the hardcore United fans have in the club’s current hierarchy.
Indeed, the Ratcliffe regime is achieving the impossible of being hated as much as the Glazers – and in less time.

The Glazers did not sack tea ladies, did not rob lifelong season-ticket holders of their seats, and would cough up whenever Ed Woodward wanted to buy another expensive dud. They’ve just been complete and utter parasites.
Ratcliffe’s promise to “put the Manchester back” into the club has brought only antipathy from their own fans and unemployment for hundreds of low-paid staff.
United have spotted a scam by ticket touts and are right to tackle it, but have done so in Ratcliffe’s brutal, heavy-handed way that is once again doing more harm than good.

Old Trafford regulars are saying they’ve never known such a split between the fans and those running the club – which is perhaps the biggest cause for concern. But then a Politburo is never meant to be popular.
Appointing Carrick is one of the few decisions they seem to have got right.
But the level-headed former midfielder could be under pressure if United don’t get three points at lowly Fulham in Sunday’s late game.
A big improvement on the hot-headed Ruben Amorim, whose “three at the back” obsession never worked, Carrick turned the club around last season.
He just needs time and fewer distractions.
One more item on his lengthening list of “smaller things” was that J.J. Gabriel, a 15-year-old jewel of the academy known as “Kid Messi”, wants to leave.
Renowned as one of the genuine wonder boys for his age and holding an Irish passport, he apparently lost patience waiting for a chance in the first team.
On October 6, his 16th birthday, he will legally be allowed to bypass UK domestic rules and sign a scholarship agreement with any major European side.
Ironically, he had been in line for an appearance against Brighton, but the boy’s father is known as a pushy character who will stop at nothing to further his son’s career.
And although United have not given up hope of keeping him, he could spark an unseemly scramble for his services from their rivals.
Real Madrid were thought to be favourites, but Barcelona, Chelsea and now City have all been mentioned. Short of joining Liverpool, City would be the hardest for United to stomach.
At least there was some joy from the youngsters with Shea Lacey, 19, becoming the first teen to score on their debut since Marcus Rashford did, aged 18, against Midtjylland in 2016.
But it was short-lived as United, showing no backbone and with a nervous debutant keeper, Karl Darlow, imploded.
The watching Carlos Baleba might have wondered if his £65m move to United from Brighton was an upgrade.
The Cameroon midfielder, who has been injured since he signed, is the latest on the Seagulls’ long list of transfer market killings. They signed him for £23m three years ago.
He should strengthen midfield but it’s defence United have to worry about. Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven are never likely to be confused with Steve Bruce and Gary Pallister.
After the loss at Hull on the opening weekend, Carrick said it was “only one game”. But it’s three defeats now in six games.
The only wins were against Ipswich and Sabah.
Carrick is right – it is cumulative, but the fans are reserving their venom for those above him.
On Wednesday, there were marches outside the ground with banners saying, "We want our club back" and "Jim ain't the one".
No, it’s not the same club anymore, not the same values.
It seems that “Kid Messi” doesn’t see a future with United either.
Which is probably the most worrying “smaller thing” of all.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

5341c4dfc68959af: PETALING JAYA: PAS dan Umno dilihat masih belum sehaluan mengenai bentuk kerjasama menerusi agenda penyatuan ummah, khususnya sama ada ia perlu membabitkan parti lain dalam Perikatan Nasional (PN), kata penganalisis.

Azmi Hassan dari Akademi Nusantara berkata pendekatan Umno setakat ini menunjukkan parti itu lebih selesa berunding secara langsung dengan PAS seperti dalam Muafakat Nasional (MN) beberapa tahun lalu.

“Penyatuan ummah secara spesifiknya bagi Umno adalah antara dengan PAS sahaja.
“Sebab itu mereka mahu berurusan dengan PAS sahaja kerana menjadi tanggungjawab PAS di dalam PN untuk membahagikan kerusi kepada rakan komponennya,” katanya kepada FMT.

Sementara itu, Tawfik Yaakub dari Universiti Malaya berkata kenyataan Timbalan Presiden PAS Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man supaya penyatuan ummah diperluaskan di luar PAS dan Umno menunjukkan parti itu perlu mengambil kira sensitiviti rakan dalam PN.

“Mana-mana formula kerjasama politik perlu lebih inklusif dan tidak mengorbankan kepentingan rakan sedia ada,” katanya.

Namun, Tawfik berkata usaha memperluaskan kerjasama itu mempunyai cabarannya tersendiri kerana semakin banyak pihak terlibat, semakin rumit rundingan berkaitan kepimpinan, pembahagian kerusi dan hala tuju hubungan dengan BN serta PN.
Katanya, kerangka lebih luas mungkin membantu PAS membina imej penyatuan Melayu-Islam yang lebih inklusif, tetapi pada masa sama membuka ruang kepada persaingan kepentingan antara parti.
Kelmarin, Tuan Ibrahim berkata PAS dan Umno perlu meluaskan agenda penyatuan ummah kepada pelbagai pihak dan tidak mengehadkan kepada hubungan antara dua parti itu semata-mata.
Beliau berkata perubahan landskap politik serta pertambahan pengundi muda menuntut satu kerangka politik lebih inklusif yang mampu merangkumi kelompok lain dalam masyarakat.
Kenyataan itu hadir ketika hubungan PAS dan Umno kembali menjadi perhatian selepas kedua-dua parti bekerjasama dalam pilihan raya negeri Negeri Sembilan.
Malah, wakil kedua-dua parti saling hadir ke Muktamar PAS dan Perhimpunan Agung Umno berlangsung bulan ini.
d7c45f78c4742854: PETALING JAYA: PAS and Umno still appear to be on different wavelengths about the form of cooperation required to "unite the ummah", particularly whether it should involve other parties in Perikatan Nasional (PN), say analysts.
Akademi Nusantara's Azmi Hassan said Umno appeared to prefer dealing directly with PAS, as it did under its now-defunct Muafakat Nasional pact.
He said the ummah unity endeavour was likely to face some hiccups if it involved PAS's PN allies, particularly opposition leader Hamzah Zainudin's Wawasan, which also vies for Malay-majority seats.
The inclusion of more parties would mean more complicated seat negotiations, especially ahead of the 16th general election, he added.
"To Umno, unity of the ummah specifically means uniting with PAS only.
"That's why they only want to deal with PAS, so that it's PAS's responsibility in PN to divide seats among its coalition partners," he told FMT.
Tawfik Yaakub of Universiti Malaya said PAS was trying to account for its PN partners, including new additions like Wawasan and Pejuang.

However, he said the pact faced a conundrum. He said the push for ummah unity should not be focused on PAS and Umno alone, as it could cause the perception that other parties in PN are only supporting acts and can be sidelined when major negotiations take place.
"Any formula for political cooperation needs to be inclusive, without sacrificing the interests of partners," he said.

He also said that expanding the cooperation to more parties would lead to tougher negotiations in terms of key leadership roles, seat allocations and the direction of Barisan Nasional (BN) and PN's relationship.
A wider cooperation model could help PAS build a more inclusive Malay unity image, but lead to conflicting interests between parties, he said.
Earlier this week, PAS deputy president Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man said PAS and Umno needed to expand their ummah unity agenda to more parties instead of limiting it to themselves.
Tuan Ibrahim argued that the shifting political landscape and entry of young voters demanded a more inclusive political framework.
BN and PAS-led PN formed an alliance in the Negeri Sembilan election which secured a two-thirds majority in the state assembly.
The rekindling of ties between Umno and PAS saw leaders of both parties attending each other's annual general assemblies earlier this month.
Umno deputy president Mohamad Hasan however said the party must spearhead any cooperation to forge Malay-Muslim political unity, and that Umno had been deceived by others in past efforts.
0b3b870ea3ad8cab: IPOH: More than 25 years have passed since Sgt Maj Zol’aini Sabar was deployed to Bukit Jenalik, but many details of the operation remain vivid.

The former 69 Commando member was among 20 personnel sent in during Op Subuh in 2000. The special operation was mounted after members of the Al-Maunah militant group stole firearms and ammunition from a territorial army camp in Gerik and retreated to Bukit Jenalik near Sauk.

For Zol’aini, now 68, the danger did not come only from the terrain, even though the area was surrounded by rubber plantations and dense undergrowth, making movement difficult and creating the risk of ambush.
More unsettling, he said, was the knowledge that some of those inside had security-force experience of their own.
“One of them was Zahit Muslim, the right-hand man of the group’s leader, Mohd Amin Razali,” Zol’aini, who is from Kampung Kepayang in Ipoh, told Bernama.
"Zahit was a former colleague of mine in the 69 Commando and was highly skilled in handling heavy weapons and booby traps.”
That familiarity made the operation especially tense. The main and support teams had been given strict instructions to apprehend all 27 members of the group alive and, if possible, avoid bloodshed.
This meant every movement had to be measured: "It required us to act with the utmost caution."
The operation nevertheless came at a heavy cost. Detective Corporal R Sanghadevan of the Special Branch and Malaysian Armed Forces commando trooper Mathew Medan were killed during the incident.
For Zol’aini, the experience changed the way he understood strength. Difficult situations, he learnt, may require restraint, judgement and a willingness to prioritise human life.

Today, he believes those lessons remain relevant beyond the battlefield. “People may not be able to imagine the tense times we went through. That is why we must never take the peace we have for granted," he said.
The memories of Bukit Jenalik also remind him how quickly a situation can deteriorate when trust and social cohesion begin to fray.
But rather than dwell on the danger, he prefers to remember the responsibility carried by those involved, including the instruction to bring the operation to an end without unnecessary loss of life.

For the father of four, that remains one of the clearest lessons he carried out of Bukit Jenalik. Protecting a country is not only about confronting threats, but also about knowing when caution, restraint and unity matter just as much as force.
74fcc919eb1bd63b: WASHINGTON: The White House on Thursday withdrew its nominee to head US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency tasked with carrying out President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

d755c7249141c504: PETALING JAYA: A plan for a waste-to-energy (WTE) plant in Batu Arang has raised concerns among residents in the area, but an expert in waste management has given an assurance that there is nothing to worry about.
Academic Agamuthu Pitchiah said that while the residents’ misgivings are valid, modern WTE plants have been designed to contain the risks that they fear.
The residents’ worries revolve around the Sultan Idris Shah (SIS) Green Energy Plant for which the environmental impact assessment (EIA) has been approved recently.
Despite the latest development, the residents have vowed to continue their protest, insisting that the plant could cause pollution.
The project is to be developed by KDEB Waste Management in collaboration with YTL Power International.

Zulfaizi Rusli, 40, who was born and raised in Batu Arang, told FMT there are concerns that while the lorries are transporting the garbage to the plant, dirty water could leak onto the roads and then drains into the rivers that flow through the district.
Sungai Garing and its tributary Sungai Batu Arang flow through the district. The area surrounding these two rivers is a popular destination for hikers and cycling enthusiasts.

Longtime resident Rusli Sharif, 71, fears that odour emanating from the garbage could also have a negative impact on tourism. “We are also worried that the air quality may be affected,” Rusli, who has lived in Batu Arang for the past half century, said.
Zulfaizi, a father of three, said there also are concerns that frequent entry of heavy vehicles into the area could damage the roads.
For musician Hashiamaldin Bazin, 58, any word on the project only brings back memories of the foul smell emanating from nearby pig farms. He fears the waste facility could cause the same problem.
Pig rearing operations in the area ceased in the 1980s, driven by several factors, including efforts to curb the widespread discharge of untreated animal waste and water pollution.
Hashiamaldin expressed doubts that anything could be done to neutralise the stench from the waste that will now come in to feed the WTE plant.
He stressed that residents do not object to technology, but they just want to be assured that it will not have a negative impact on them.
For Rusli, it comes down to a simple matter: “How do you expect people to come to your heritage town if you have an incinerator?”

Agamuthu, a senior professor at the Jeffrey Sachs Center on Sustainable Development at Sunway University, said ordinary incinerators and WTE plants are often grouped together because both involve combustion.
An incinerator, he explained, is a combustion chamber, but the difference between a traditional plant and a WTE plant lies in energy generation and the safeguards during combustion.
He said modern WTE facilities are designed to contain odour when waste is delivered to the plant.
“They use what is called negative pressure. The moment the door opens for the lorry to offload, the vacuum inside will actually suck the air in from outside.
“As the air is sucked in, so is the odour,” he told FMT.
Agamuthu said there also are systems in place that will treat any emission released through the combustion process to ensure it is no longer harmful.

For instance, he said, when plastic is burned, toxic chemicals may be released, but modern WTE plants are designed with new technology such as catalytic converters and fibre filters, to remove those chemicals.
“Ultimately, modern WTE facilities are subject to detailed assessment on the same issues raised by residents, including proximity to homes, odour and lorry movement,” Agamuthu stressed.

“Any waste to energy plant has to go through a detailed environmental impact assessment (EIA). Experts will review the EIA and look into all these issues such as proximity to houses or lorry transportation,” he said, adding that a detailed EIA is prepared by both government officers and experts in air pollution and traffic control, among others.

The proposal for the WTE plant was first mooted in 2019. In a 2023 response to protests against the project, Selangor menteri besar Amirudin Shari said it would not be like “incinerators from the 1990s” as it would not use old technology.
The plant is designed to process up to 2,400 tonnes of municipal wastes daily to help alleviate pressure on overflowing landfills across six local councils in Selangor.
8469d136d0518e7c: PETALING JAYA: Rancangan pembinaan loji sisa pepejal kepada tenaga (WTE) di Batu Arang menimbulkan kebimbangan penduduk, namun pakar pengurusan sisa memberi jaminan tiada apa perlu dirisaukan.
Ahli akademik, Agamuthu Pariatamby, berkata walaupun kebimbangan penduduk berasas, loji WTE moden direka bentuk untuk mengawal dan membendung risiko.
Kebimbangan penduduk terarah kepada Loji Tenaga Hijau Sultan Idris Shah (SIS) yang baru-baru ini mendapat kelulusan penilaian impak alam sekitar (EIA).
Walaupun dengan perkembangan terbaru itu, penduduk berikrar akan meneruskan bantahan dan menegaskan loji tersebut berpotensi menyebabkan pencemaran.
Projek itu akan dibangunkan oleh KDEB Waste Management dengan kerjasama YTL Power International.

Anak jadi Batu Arang, Zulfaizi Rusli, 40, memberitahu FMT wujud kebimbangan air kotor daripada sampah yang dibawa oleh lori ke loji itu boleh tertumpah ke jalan raya sebelum mengalir ke sungai yang merentasi daerah tersebut.

Sungai Garing dan anak sungainya, Sungai Batu Arang, mengalir merentasi daerah tersebut. Kawasan di sekitar kedua-dua sungai itu adalah destinasi popular bagi penggemar aktiviti mendaki dan berbasikal.
Rusli Sharif, 71, bimbang bau yang berpunca daripada sampah boleh memberi kesan negatif terhadap sektor pelancongan.
"Kami juga bimbang kualiti udara mungkin terjejas,” katanya yang menetap di Batu Arang lebih 50 tahun.
Zulfaizi, bapa kepada tiga anak berkata kemasukan kenderaan berat yang kerap ke kawasan itu dikhuatiri boleh menyebabkan jalan raya rosak.

Bagi pemuzik, Hashiamaldin Bazin, 58, berita mengenai projek itu hanya mengembalikan ingatan kepada bau busuk dari ladang babi berhampiran. Dia bimbang kemudahan pengurusan sisa tersebut akan menyebabkan masalah sama.
Aktiviti penternakan babi di kawasan itu dihentikan pada 1980-an kerana beberapa faktor termasuk usaha membendung pelepasan sisa haiwan yang tidak dirawat dan pencemaran air.
Hashiamaldin mempersoalkan sama ada bau busuk daripada sisa buangan yang akan dibawa masuk ke loji WTE itu mampu dinyahbau atau dikawal sepenuhnya.
Beliau menegaskan, penduduk tidak menolak teknologi sebaliknya hanya mahu jaminan ia tidak akan memberi kesan negatif kepada mereka.
Bagi Rusli, ia berpunca daripada satu persoalan mudah: "Bagaimana anda mahu orang datang ke bandar warisan jika ada sebuah insinerator?"

Agamuthu yang juga profesor kanan di Pusat Pembangunan Mampan Jeffrey Sachs Sunway University berkata, insinerator biasa dan WTE sering dikategorikan bersama kerana kedua-duanya melibatkan proses pembakaran.
Beliau menjelaskan, insinerator ialah ruang pembakaran, namun perbezaan antara loji tradisional dan WTE adalah pada penjanaan tenaga serta langkah keselamatan semasa proses pembakaran.
Katanya, kemudahan WTE moden direka bentuk untuk mengekang bau apabila sisa dihantar ke loji tersebut.
"Teknologi yang digunakan dipanggil tekanan negatif. Apabila pintu dibuka untuk lori menurunkan muatan, vakum di dalam akan menyedut udara dari luar.
"Udara disedut masuk, begitu juga dengan bau,” katanya kepada FMT.
Agamuthu berkata, terdapat juga sistem yang akan merawat sebarang pelepasan terhasil daripada proses pembakaran bagi memastikan ia tidak lagi memudaratkan.

Katanya, sebagai contoh apabila plastik dibakar, bahan kimia toksik mungkin terhasil, namun loji WTE moden direka dengan teknologi baharu seperti penukar pemangkin dan penapis gentian untuk menyingkirkan bahan tersebut.
"Pada akhirnya, kemudahan WTE moden tertakluk kepada penilaian terperinci terhadap isu yang sama dibangkitkan penduduk, termasuk jarak dengan kawasan perumahan, bau dan pergerakan lori," katanya.

"Mana-mana loji sisa kepada tenaga perlu melalui EIA yang terperinci. Pakar akan menilai EIA tersebut dan meneliti semua isu seperti jarak dengan rumah atau pengangkutan lori," katanya memaklumkan EIA terperinci disediakan pegawai kerajaan serta pakar dalam pencemaran udara dan kawalan trafik.

Cadangan loji WTE itu mula dikemukakan pada 2019. Dalam maklum balas pada 2023 terhadap bantahan projek tersebut, Menteri Besar Selangor Amirudin Shari berkata ia tidak sama seperti 'insinerator pada 1990-an' kerana tidak menggunakan teknologi lama.
Loji itu direka untuk memproses sehingga 2,400 tan sisa domestik sehari bagi membantu mengurangkan masalah tapak pelupusan sampah yang semakin penuh di enam pihak berkuasa tempatan Selangor.
23c598a12a10cd9b: BUENOS AIRES: Argentine President Javier Milei on Thursday sent a bill to Congress that toughens sanctions for British-authorised oil projects in the disputed Falkland Islands.
The measure comes amid heightened tensions between Britain and Argentina over the South Atlantic archipelago, over which the two countries fought a brief but bitter war in 1982.
Argentina refers to the British overseas territory as Las Malvinas and claims them as an integral part of its land, which London rejects.

Milei has toughened Argentina's claim to the archipelago after President Donald Trump recently threatened to review Washington's neutrality in the dispute, in what was seen as a warning to the British government to align itself with his agenda.

Milei has focused his ire on a UK-Israeli oil project near the islands, arguing it violates a United Nations rule against any unilateral actions in the islands pending the resolution of the territorial dispute.

The Argentine government's draft "Law for the Defence of National Sovereignty" published Thursday prohibits the exploitation of any natural resources in the Falklands, not just oil, without authorisation from Buenos Aires.
It raises the penalty set out in a 2011 law from a maximum of 15 years in prison to 20 years imprisonment.
The bill is largely seen as symbolic, however.
London does not recognise the jurisdiction of Argentine courts in the Falklands.

The companies developing a major oil field off the Falklands, Israel's Navitas and Britain's Rockhopper, have shrugged off Argentina's threats, insisting they have valid exploration licences issued by the United Kingdom.
The Falkland Islanders themselves voted overwhelmingly in 2013 to remain British.
But Argentina rejects that outcome, arguing that the principle of self-determination does not apply to a population it considers implanted by Britain after 1833.
2b51d7bece67a8d2: BERA: Five police reports have been lodged by Orang Asli villagers following a viral incident involving an enforcement team member who allegedly kicked a burning incense pot at Kampung Pathir here on Sept 15.
The incident occurred during a joint enforcement operation at the Tasek Bera Conservation Forest Reserve (Ramsar) site.
District police chief Superintendent Zulkiflee Nazir said the reports were lodged by Orang Asli villagers living near the Tasek Bera between Sept 15 and Wednesday.
"The Orang Asli lodged reports claiming that an individual who was part of the enforcement operation had kicked a sacred object belonging to the community.
"We will record statements from the five complainants, the individual involved and other enforcement team members who were present during the incident," he said when contacted yesterday.
Zulkiflee said the case was being investigated under Section 295 of the Penal Code for defiling a sacred object, which carries a maximum two-year jail sentence.

In the video, an individual is seen kicking the burning incense pot, which had been left in the middle of the road, towards the roadside. The action sparked anger among members of the Orang Asli community who were present at the site.
The villagers claimed that the burning incense pot, known as a tengkarang, was used by the community to offer prayers and perform certain rituals.
The community shared a video of the incident on social media saying that the pot was part of their beliefs and heritage, and that such an action could not be tolerated.

It is learnt that members of the enforcement team had earlier asked the villagers to remove the pot, but they refused. This prompted an officer to push it away with his leg while the pot was still burning.
49a9d1848ea91ce6: SAN FRANCISCO: OpenAI committed "an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions" when it used millions of news articles to train its artificial intelligence models, the New York Times alleged in a court document unsealed on Thursday.
The San Francisco-based artificial intelligence lab scraped content from more than 10 million articles, nearly a third of which came from the New York Times alone.
The document claims Microsoft's director of applied science Brent Hect called it "an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions" and possibly the "largest theft of labour in human history."

Hect also allegedly warned that OpenAI might have engaged in an "accidental cover up" in its attempts to identify content in its systems that came from the New York Times and the lawsuit's other plaintiffs.

The newspaper sued OpenAI and Microsoft three years ago in New York federal court for allegedly stealing its copyrighted material to train OpenAI's flagship model, ChatGPT. Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019.

Several other news publishers also joined the lawsuit, including Ziff Davis - which owns CNET and other tech news publications - as well as the parent company of the magazine Mother Jones, the investigative news site The Intercept, and multiple local newspapers across the United States.
They are seeking damages for each article that was allegedly stolen and used by OpenAI's models, though it is unclear what the total amount of penalties could reach.

OpenAI has signed content licensing deals with many news publishers around the world since it launched ChatGPT in late 2022, but concerns persist that generative AI software is reducing traffic to internet news sites.
AI companies have tried to alleviate those concerns by adding citations with links to user queries, but the effort has been criticised as insufficient.
"No matter how prominently we show the links, users won't click," one of OpenAI's own engineers admitted, according to the court document.
Microsoft and OpenAI argue that their use of news content is transformative and falls under "fair use" laws.
In early September, the US department of justice filed a brief in support of OpenAI and Microsoft, in which it invoked "scientific progress," economic growth, and "national security."
The plaintiffs have requested a summary judgement in their favor.
If granted by US district judge Sidney Stein, the case would not go to trial, but a ruling is not expected until 2027.
514848d09f6d2b09: KUANTAN: The Pahang government is prepared to assist Orang Asli living near Tasek Bera, but delays in providing a list of residents in the settlements have hampered efforts to help them.

Pahang Islamic Religious Affairs, Rural Development and Orang Asli Affairs Committee chairman Datuk Seri Syed Ibrahim Syed Ahmad said there were more than seven villages near the lake, but only one had submitted the required list.
He said during a visit to several Orang Asli settlements near the lake on Aug 3, that he had assured the villagers that the state government wanted to help them continue earning a livelihood.

"I told the Orang Asli families living and earning a livelihood within the Tasek Bera forest reserve to provide a list of residents and details of their smallholdings before we can negotiate on their behalf.

"So far, only villagers from Kampung Lubuk Tihang have provided the details to the Orang Asli Development Department (Jakoa). The other villagers have yet to submit the requested information, and they can still do so.
"Jakoa has gone to the villages three times to request the list," he told the New Straits Times.

The NST reported that some 7,000 Orang Asli villagers living near the lake are seeking negotiations with the authorities after receiving notices in June ordering them to vacate parts of the forest reserve. They were alleged to have encroached into the Tasek Bera Conservation Forest Reserve.

After receiving the notices, the villagers set up guard posts at all village entrances and smallholdings around Tasek Bera to prevent outsiders, including enforcement personnel, from entering. This led to the arrest of five villagers on Sept 15.

Meanwhile, Syed Ibrahim said the list was vital for Jakoa to obtain details of those living in the area, including the locations and sizes of their homes and farms, as well as the number of family members, so that their applications could be assessed.
He said the information would enable the state government to identify genuine residents and determine how it could assist them, including through discussions on the land.
"When I say we (the Pahang government) want to help, it means we will go and negotiate on their behalf. We are ready to assist those affected.

"We understand that the villagers have been occupying land located within a forest reserve and Ramsar site, but they cannot claim to be the landowners simply because they have been living there for a long time," he said.
Syed Ibrahim said the list of names and locations would also allow the authorities to determine which sections of the land could potentially be gazetted for the villagers.
"We have a system. We do not want the villagers to continue living scattered throughout the forest reserve without proper documentation," he said.

When asked about the delay in submitting the names, Syed Ibrahim expressed concern that outsiders might be taking advantage of the situation by occupying land illegally or manipulating the Orang Asli community.

"Initially, the villagers agreed to submit the information but later did not cooperate. It is difficult to understand why they would not want to provide their names... there might be someone influencing them," he said.
The NST has reached out to Kampung Pathir Tok Batin Amir Noor Tan for comment.
