06495e6069670959: SHAH ALAM, Sept 18 — Inside a closed-house chicken farm in Jalan Kebun here, Mohd Muzamri Shoib instructed one of his workers to open the door.
He chose the worker deliberately.
As the door opened, Muzamri watched the flock before explaining why even a simple interruption to their routine could cause stress.
“These chickens can get stressed when someone they do not recognise opens the door,” he said.
But an unfamiliar presence is not the only source of stress for the birds.
Heat poses a far more serious challenge, and one that farmers cannot simply keep outside the door.
A prolonged spell of extreme heat could affect how quickly chickens grow, how much farmers lose and how well they perform.
Keeping the heat out
Malay Mail recently visited Muzamri’s farm, where the broiler farmer and chairman of the Selangor Poultry Farmers Association has spent 26 years raising chickens.

With a very strong El Niño expected to develop towards the end of this year, Malaysia could face extreme heat and dry weather from January to May 2027, with temperatures potentially reaching 40°C, according to MetMalaysia.
Farmers like Muzamri are therefore relying on systems that have become an increasingly important part of modern poultry farming.
His farm has two closed-house poultry buildings, one with two levels and another with a single level, both equipped with cooling pads and exhaust fans designed to keep temperatures under control.
The cooling pads line the walls of the buildings, with water pumped from large tanks and circulated through them before air is drawn through and cooled.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Muzamri inside his closed-house chicken farm in Jalan Kebun, Shah Alam. — Picture by Yusof Isa
At the other end, large exhaust fans pull the air out while helping to remove ammonia and odours from the building.
The result is a controlled environment in which the temperature can be adjusted according to the age of the chickens.
Younger birds, for instance, require warmer conditions, with temperatures of around 37°C being more comfortable for them, similar to the warmth they would experience with a mother hen.
For older broilers, however, excessive heat becomes a growing concern.
When chickens start to overheat

Professor Datuk Zulkifli Idrus, director of the Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Food Security at Universiti Putra Malaysia, said chickens were particularly vulnerable to prolonged heat because they could not sweat like humans.
Their bodies are covered with feathers, making it harder for them to lose heat.
Instead, chickens mainly cool themselves by panting and increasing blood flow to their skin, combs and wattles.
“When temperatures remain high, they pant more, become less active, eat less and drink more,” he said.
If the heat continues, the birds can become dehydrated and their normal bodily functions can be disrupted.
Severe and prolonged heat stress can eventually result in organ failure and death, Zulkifli said.
For broiler farmers, the problem is compounded by the birds’ rapid growth.
Modern broilers become heavy quickly and generate considerable body heat, making birds approaching market weight particularly vulnerable when temperatures rise.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Broiler chickens at Muzamri’s closed-house chicken farm. — Picture by Yusof Isa
Cooling the flock
Muzamri said his farm’s environmental control system allows him to regulate the temperature, ventilation and feeding of the chickens.
The system is currently operated through controls at the farm, although he is looking to upgrade it so the same functions can be managed through a smartphone.
That would allow him to monitor and adjust the system even when he is away from the farm.
The controls can be used for the chicken feeders, cooling pads and fans.
And when the heat becomes particularly intense, Muzamri has another measure ready.
He buys bags of ice and puts them into a reservoir through which water passes before being pumped towards the cooling pads.
He normally orders about 30 large bags, which he said can last five to six days.
The farm has about eight water tanks, roughly the size of those commonly found in the attics of Malaysian landed homes.
Heat stress on chickens
For Muzamri, these preparations are not new.
The system has been in use for years, but the prospect of a prolonged period of extreme heat means there is little room for complacency.

“My farming activities are primarily focused on broiler chickens, but hot weather and maintaining temperatures in poultry houses are indeed very important issues for the poultry industry as a whole, particularly the broiler sector.
“When excessively hot weather occurs, chickens can experience heat stress. The effects depend on the type and age of the chickens.

“For broilers, some of the common concerns include reduced feed intake, slower growth, poorer feed conversion ratio and an increased risk of mortality if temperature and ventilation are not properly controlled,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Professor Datuk Zulkifli Idrus, director of the Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Food Security at Universiti Putra Malaysia, said chickens were particularly vulnerable to prolonged heat because they could not sweat like humans. — Picture by Yusof Isa

These systems are increasingly important for modern farmers, particularly those operating closed-house farms, where exhaust fans, cooling pads, tunnel ventilation systems, temperature and humidity sensors and automatic controllers are used to manage heat.
“When temperatures rise, these systems increase ventilation and use cooling pads to help lower the temperature inside the poultry house,” Muzamri said.
“We also incur costs to purchase ice to help cool the poultry houses during the hottest part of the day, between 11am and 3pm.”
But keeping chickens cool is not simply a matter of turning on more fans.
Water is just as important.
Zulkifli said chickens drink substantially more during hot weather as they try to replace fluids lost through panting and cool their bodies.
A constant supply of clean drinking water that is not excessively warm is therefore essential, while farmers must also ensure their generators and emergency power supplies are working.
A power failure during extreme heat can be particularly dangerous in a closed-house system because the ventilation and cooling systems can stop at the moment they are most needed.
Muzamri said his preparations also extend to giving the chickens drinks containing rock sugar and other supplements intended to help them cope with the heat.
“We also provide chickens with drinks that can help cool their bodies, including rock sugar and other additional supplements, to help regulate their body temperature,” he said.

For open-house farms, where conditions inside the poultry houses are more directly affected by the weather outside, farmers must pay closer attention to ventilation, fans, shading, water supply and stocking density.
Preparing for prolonged heat

Zulkifli said the greatest risk was not necessarily a single exceptionally hot afternoon, but a prolonged spell in which high temperatures persisted day after day, particularly when nights remained warm and gave the birds little opportunity to recover.
“The problem is not just one unusually hot afternoon, but a series of hot days over a long period, especially if the night temperatures stay high and the birds have little time to recover,” he said.
The combination of temperature, humidity, ventilation and water availability determines how severe the heat stress becomes.
Adult chickens generally begin to experience heat stress when temperatures rise above about 26°C, particularly when humidity is high, he said.
The risk becomes considerably greater once temperatures reach 32°C to 35°C and above.
High humidity makes panting less effective because the birds struggle to release heat through evaporation.
For broilers, the consequences can extend beyond animal welfare and into production.
Heat-stressed birds eat less, grow more slowly and can become less efficient at converting feed into body weight.
Severe or prolonged heat stress can also increase mortality.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Modern broilers become heavy quickly and generate considerable body heat, making birds approaching market weight particularly vulnerable when temperatures rise. — Picture by Yusof Isa
Laying hens face a different set of problems.
Reduced feed intake means fewer nutrients and less energy are available for egg production, while prolonged heat exposure can interfere with reproductive processes.
The result can be fewer and smaller eggs, as well as poorer eggshell quality.
For farmers, the priority is therefore to prevent heat stress before it becomes severe.
“Fans, cooling pads, water pumps, sensors, generators and water supplies need to be inspected and maintained more frequently,” Muzamri said.
At Muzamri’s farm, much of that infrastructure is already in place.
The technology may eventually move further away from the farm floor and into the farmer’s hand, with smartphone controls allowing Muzamri to monitor conditions and operate equipment remotely.
For now, however, the principle remains the same as it has throughout his 26 years in the industry: keep the birds comfortable, keep the air moving and make sure there is enough water.
With the heat expected to intensify, those preparations could become increasingly important.
76638fb73880b365: NEW YORK, Sept 18 — OpenAI has rattled the quiet world of mathematics by using artificial intelligence to solve a major, century-old problem, raising the question of what role mathematicians will play in scientific research going forward.
Earlier this month, thousands of its AI agents worked together to solve the Navier-Stokes equations — which generations of mathematicians have tried to tackle — in a matter of four days.

UCLA professor Terence Tao, who has won the elite Fields Medal recognising the world’s most esteemed mathematicians, told AFP: “I am currently completely overwhelmed with an existential crisis in my field.”
The recent shake-up to the field is the latest in a series of instances of AI making mathematical breakthroughs this year.

“If they did choose to study the questions that we find interesting in research, they would be very easy. They could solve those problems easily,” said Steven Strogatz, a Cornell University professor for the public understanding of science and mathematics.

Antonio Auffinger, a Northwestern University maths professor, said that just a year ago, “hallucinations were happening all the time,” but nowadays, “AI can produce long chain arguments,” without wandering off course.

In January, Elon Musk – the world’s richest man and an AI chief himself through SpaceXAI – predicted mathematics would be “crushed,” saying “math is going to be extremely trivial for AI” on a podcast.

Yet, while Northwestern University maths professor Benjamin Antieau said there is “awe and amazement” for the feat, “in this particular case, they were following in the footsteps of other mathematicians who’d been developing this programmatic approach to this particular class of problems for many, many years.”

In this case, the AI mainly followed two Spanish researchers, who were also the inspiration for mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpoge — who claim they came close to the solution before OpenAI’s breakthrough and are now questioning if their work was plagiarised — a charge the AI tech giant denies.
‘Leaps of creativity’
That’s not the only issue with OpenAI’s calculations.
“The flag is captured, the goal scored, and the problem is solved; but at the cost of lessons learned, insights gained, collaborations formed, and new targets located,” Tao wrote on Mastodon.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

UCLA mathematics professor Terence Tao, a Fields Medal winner, warns that recent advances in artificial intelligence are raising difficult questions about the future role of mathematicians. — AFP file pic
Tao was among 25 Fields Medal laureates who signed a letter last Friday to warn of a potential “destructive effect” by AI on the field of mathematics.
To boot, Stanford University professor Mohammed Abouzaid said the technology’s lack of imagination is apparent.

“We are still not seeing the kind of leaps of creativity that really involve creating new mathematics, and maybe the labs are going to make that their next target, and that would be very interesting to see,” Abouzaid said.

Anima Anandkumar, a Caltech professor working at the intersection of mathematics and AI, succeeded with her team in solving a simplified form of the Navier-Stokes equations (known as Euler equations) using an AI model that did not rely on prior works from researchers.
This AI was not like the ones powering ChatGPT or Claude, but rather a physics-informed neural network (PINN) model, which combines data with the laws of physics.
“So, you could think of OpenAI as being more reliant on humans than we are in some sense,” she said.
However, Anandkumar notes that the model still had to be designed and tested.

Auffinger said he does not foresee a time when AI tools “would be able to provide answers for any questions that you ask” and that human mathematicians will continue to “play a huge role because it’s not about how to go from point A to point B.”
“It’s about asking the questions that will help society as a whole,” he explained. — AFP
c48b2b0f6650fb58: SUBANG JAYA, Sept 18 — Brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease were found to begin 15 to 20 years before the onset of noticeable memory loss, making long-term sleep hygiene a critical and early preventive measure.

Sunway Medical Centre, Sunway City Consultant Neurologist Dr Mohamad Imran Idris warned that while pulling occasional late nights might have seemed harmless, consistent poor sleep patterns over months and years compounded metabolic stress on the brain, accelerating neurodegenerative risks.

“Changes in the brain start 15 to 20 years before somebody actually develops dementia, meaning 20 years before they start having severe memory problems, you can already see microscopic changes occurring,” he told Bernama in an exclusive interview.
Addressing a widespread biological misconception, Dr Mohamad Imran emphasised that individuals could not compensate for or “buy back” lost weekday sleep by oversleeping during weekends.

“Sleep regularity is what matters because pulling four-hour nights and trying to compensate with 12-hour weekend sleep simply does not work biologically to clear accumulated brain inflammation,” he explained.
He noted that during deep sleep, the brain actively clears away metabolic waste, cellular debris and inflammation accumulated during waking hours.
Chronic sleep deprivation, he noted, deprives the brain of this essential recovery window, thereby increasing the risk of cognitive decline over time.

Dr Mohamad Imran highlighted a distinct U-shaped correlation between sleep duration and dementia risk, noting that the biological sweet spot for brain recovery was seven to eight hours of uninterrupted sleep per night.

“Too little sleep increases the risk of dementia, but too much sleep can also reflect that someone is already developing it, especially if someone who used to sleep normally suddenly begins sleeping for much longer hours or stays in bed all day,” he noted.

In terms of risk demographics, he pointed out that gender played a significant role, with statistics showing there were approximately twice as many women as men over the age of 65 living with Alzheimer’s disease.
Sunway Medical Centre neurologist Dr Mohamad Imran Idris says brain changes can begin 15 to 20 years before dementia symptoms appear. — Bernama pic
He further explained that up to a decade before a formal diagnosis, subtle non-cognitive indicators often emerged, including rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder.
He said this condition involved individuals lacking normal dream-state muscle paralysis, causing them to physically act out vivid dreams through shouting, punching or kicking in their sleep.

In Malaysia, dementia prevalence was shown to be escalating alongside an ageing demographic, with Health Ministry surveys indicating that approximately 10 per cent of Malaysians over 60 suffered from the condition, rising to 33 per cent among those aged 80 and above.

Despite these sobering figures, Dr Mohamad Imran stressed that modern diagnostics, such as blood-based biomarkers combined with newly approved disease-modifying therapies, now allow specialists to actively slow down the physical progression of the disease.

He said that healthier lifestyle changes, such as managing cardiovascular health, staying physically active, cognitive training with stimulation activities to challenge the brain, avoiding smoking, reducing exposure to air pollution, and maintaining social engagement with people around, help in delaying the early onset of Alzheimer’s symptoms.

“If you notice a persistent change in your sleeping patterns or are becoming unusually forgetful, see a doctor early, because waiting until memory problems prevent you from recognising family members is often too late,” he urged.
World Alzheimer’s Day, observed globally every year on Sept 21, continued to serve as a vital platform to raise international awareness and advocate for early medical intervention. — Bernama
cd146dd27dcaed0d: HYDERABAD, Sept 18 — When transgender woman Kali Sidharth Medepalli began hormone replacement therapy in India, she expected to complete her medical transition and undergo surgery within a year.
But just months after she began treatment earlier this year, India’s parliament amended the country’s transgender law, and the clinic where she was receiving care stopped her medicines.
“Everything shut down,” the 23-year-old communications specialist and LGBTQ rights activist told AFP in the southern city of Hyderabad.
Kali said she went 10 days without a testosterone blocker, experiencing hot flushes and body aches.
The amendment introduced penalties for forcing someone to assume a transgender identity through surgical, chemical or hormonal procedures.
Authorities say the changes are meant to better protect vulnerable groups by strengthening penalties for exploitation, forced identity and trafficking.
The government said it does not criminalise consensual, medically supervised care, but activists and doctors say the amendment created uncertainty for thousands of people.
“The healthcare system is very fearful right now,” said transgender rights activist Vyjayanti Vasanta Mogli, a member of a Supreme Court advisory committee on transgender welfare.
The lack of clarity, she said, could “scare away even the ones who have the best interests for the trans people”.
Kali later managed to obtain her medicine using her existing prescription but was forced to self-medicate.
“Ideally, you should have a doctor doing this for you,” she said.
Doctor’s dilemma
The case illustrates the dilemma facing transgender people seeking safe medical care, said Sanjay Sharma, head of the Association for Transgender Health in India.
Doctors face a choice. Continuing treatment could expose them to legal risk, but refusing care could conflict with their medical responsibilities.
“How can I refuse care? I took an oath that above all do no harm,” said Sharma, a doctor and retired airforce commodore.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Transgender rights activist Vyjayanti Vasanta Mogli speaks to AFP in Hyderabad during an interview after the Indian parliament amended the country’s law and introduced penalties for forcing someone to assume a transgender identity through surgical, chemical or hormonal procedures while saying it does not criminalise consensual, medically supervised care. — AFP pic
Some private clinics have continued treatment but are taking extra precautions, including additional paperwork, consent forms and charging patients more.
“Private clinics will now give care, but they lawyer up,” Sharma said.
It is particularly difficult for people without supportive families, established doctors or money for private care.
Mumbai-based Meghna Kulkarni, who supports her child’s transition, said the amendment “immediately rang danger bells”, but unlike others, they had a support network.
“We already knew the doctors, the surgeon, the psychiatrist,” Kulkarni said.
There are no official figures for how many transgender people receive gender-affirming healthcare in India, making the scale of the disruption difficult to assess.
India does not have a current estimate of its transgender population.
While India’s official 2011 Census recorded roughly 488,000 transgender individuals, human rights groups and experts estimate that the actual population is between five and six million people.
Uneven access
The uncertainty over the amendment also affects transgender identity certification.
Bhukya Ahalya, 21, who transitioned in 2025, wants regular employment but has struggled to update her identity documents, which still identify her as a man.
She now survives by begging at traffic signals.
“Everyone wants me to move on from this life,” she said. “But when I want to move on, when I want to earn a respectful life, I don’t get a TG (transgender) card.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Transgender woman Bhukya Ahalya, 21, transitioned when she was 20 and struggles to update her identity documents, which still identify her as a man, making it difficult for her to get stable employment. — AFP pic
The government website for applying for a transgender identity card — the first step towards changing other key documents — has not functioned since the amendment came into force.
The amendment has added an extra layer of scrutiny to the process. Now a designated medical board must recommend certification, after which a magistrate can issue the identity certificate.
The amendment is being challenged in the Supreme Court. Petitioners cite constitutional protections including dignity, autonomy and privacy, as well as the right to self-identification.
AFP contacted the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment for clarification on the amendment, its rules and the identity-card portal, but received no response.
For Kali, her carefully planned medical transition has become uncertain.
“I don’t know the future,” she said. “I can’t plan it anymore”. — AFP
770f03f0b1da2f77: KAPUAS HULU, Sept 18 — Indonesian villager Octavius wades through the forest in rubber boots and tattered joggers, ears pricked, eyes peeled, a telephoto lens on his phone primed to capture orangutans, monkeys or birds.
The daily photo hunt earns Octavius and hundreds of others in Borneo cash as part of a conservation programme seeking to make animals worth more alive than dead.
Locals on the island have long made money from hunting wild songbirds and selling them, mainly to domestic customers.
The KehatiKu project aims to break that cycle by paying individuals in nine participating villages in West Kalimantan province for photos or recordings of animals instead.
Payments range from 5,000 rupiah (about US$0.30/RM1.26) for observing a common bird, to 130,000 rupiah (about RM32.80) for an endangered orangutan — the top prize.
The most successful observers earn up to 10 million rupiah a month — equivalent to about US$570 (RM2,410), several times an average farmworker’s income.
The extra cash “really helps, especially to pay for my children’s college”, said 50-year-old Octavius, who like many Indonesians uses a single name.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Imam Mujiono, biodiversity field project coordinator for Borneo Future Indonesia, searches for targeted animals in West Kalimantan, Indonesia on September 2, 2026. — AFP pic
The programme, run by environmental consultancy Borneo Futures, began two years ago and produces data on wildlife distribution and population changes.
Most participants are small-scale farmers of rice, cacao, durian and the stimulant kratom.
Early signs suggest the scheme is working.

“People have started to realise that where previously they caught one bird and it was worth 50,000 rupiah, now they just need to take a photo, send it to us, and they can receive a payment of 5,000 to 10,000 rupiah,” Borneo Futures Indonesia director Nardiyono told AFP.

“If they take just five photos, they (may) earn 50,000 rupiah, and the bird is still in their environment, still observable, and still able to reproduce, so the potential income from observing birds is far greater than from hunting birds.”
Side-job
That shifting logic has prompted two participating villages to voluntarily introduce hunting bans since the project started, added Nardiyono.
The programme is funded by philanthropic foundations and has received about US$300,000 (RM1.27 million) to date, according to Borneo Futures.
Half has gone towards development, including a mobile app for uploading animal sightings and an AI system that helps humans verify observations.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Borneo Future Indonesia wildlife observer Diyonisius receiving payment for observation activities in Labian village in Kapuas Hulu, West Kalimantan. Indonesian as part of a conservation programme seeking to make animals worth more alive than dead. — AFP pic
So far, users have submitted over 350,000 observations, about half of which have been validated and paid for.
Invalid entries might include multiple observations of the same animal, or a species that is not on the programme’s list.
In September, Octavius and dozens of others gathered at the tiny office in Labian village – population 683 – for their monthly payments.
His share was four million rupiah, or nearly US$230 (RM970).
“This is a side-job; it doesn’t interfere” with farming, he told AFP as he showed off a patch where he grows kratom and cacao.

“Sometimes when we’re working, when everyone is gathered to collect kratom leaves, we hear birds calling, so we go over, observe them — if we can take a photo, we take a photo; if not, we just make a sound recording.”

The programme’s model is “likely better for both environmental and social impacts than an unincentivised, top-down conservation project design,” said researcher Paul Ferraro of the US-based Johns Hopkins University.
The main challenge will be maintaining funding, he added.
“People may revert to their prior behavioural patterns because the incentive payments are insufficient when the enthusiasm has waned,” said Ferraro, an expert in human behaviour and public policy.
Sense of independence
For now, Borneo Futures has funding secured through 2028, and two more villages will join next month.
It pays for observations of 73 species, including birds, monkeys, wild cats and deer.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Erik Meijaard (left), managing director of Borneo Future, and Nardiyono (right), director of Borneo Future Indonesia, talk about a new conservation programme to rope in local villagers during a session in Sungai Ajung village in Kapuas Hulu, West Kalimantan on September 2, 2026. — AFP pic
Antonia Uneng says she never has to venture too far from her home in Sungai Ajung, a village of fewer than 400 people, for observations.
She bought her first fridge with her earnings, as well as a karaoke machine, complete with flashing lights and two microphones, that occupies pride of place in her living room.
The project has given women in the village a sense of independence, said the 36-year-old part-time nursing assistant, whose husband works abroad.
“I have my own income... so I am not dependent on my husband.”
Imelda, a farmer in Labian, goes into the forest daily with friends to record bird sounds and, if they are lucky, orangutans.
“It makes us healthier, walking in the forest,” said the 72-year-old.
In the past, some in the community considered wild boar and deer pests for damaging their gardens and crops, she said.
But now, “we really, really want to protect them”. — AFP
d3104f5b02ea2fe7: From Selvam Shanmugam
The continuing public differences between Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and deputy prime minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi now require political clarity.

There is nothing improper about disagreement within a coalition government. But Zahid is not merely the president of Umno. He is also the deputy prime minister and a member of the Cabinet, and that office carries collective responsibility.
If Zahid believes his differences with the direction of the government have become fundamental, the proper course would be for him to consider relinquishing his executive positions.
If, on the other hand, Anwar concludes that Zahid can no longer effectively remain in his administration, the prime minister should be prepared to act.
The Federal Constitution provides a clear framework.

Article 43(3) establishes collective Cabinet responsibility, while Article 43(5) deals with the tenure of ministers and provides for the revocation of a minister’s appointment by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong on the advice of the prime minister.
Any such removal would concern Zahid’s executive office. It would not, by itself, require him to vacate his parliamentary seat.

An important legal qualification must be made: political disagreement or public criticism does not automatically amount to a loss of constitutional confidence, nor does Article 43 automatically require a minister to resign merely because he publicly disagrees with the prime minister.
The decisive issue arises only if the political disagreement affects Anwar’s majority in the Dewan Rakyat.
If Umno continues to support Anwar, the government may continue so long as the prime minister commands the confidence of the majority.

If Umno withdraws its support and Anwar consequently ceases to command the confidence of the majority, Article 43(4) requires the prime minister to tender the resignation of the Cabinet unless Parliament is dissolved at his request.
Any request for dissolution remains subject to the Yang di-Pertuan Agong’s discretion under Article 40(2)(b).
That is the real test: Does Anwar continue to command the confidence of the majority of the Dewan Rakyat?
If Zahid believes the government’s direction is no longer one he can support from within the Cabinet, he should consider stepping aside from executive office.

If Anwar believes Zahid’s position is incompatible with continued Cabinet service, he should have the courage to make that decision and allow Umno to state clearly whether it continues to support his government.
This is not a call for instability. It is a call for clarity and accountability.
Let Zahid decide whether he remains part of the government. Let Anwar decide whether Zahid should remain in his Cabinet. Then let Umno and the parliamentary numbers speak for themselves.
Malaysia should not remain trapped in prolonged political ambiguity.
Selvam Shanmugam is an advocate and solicitor at the High Court of Malaya.

b13fe3ee1cc5d4d4: PETALING JAYA: In 2017, Malaysian-born Jolene Loh walked away from a corporate career in companies like Microsoft, Yahoo and The Walt Disney Company.

Based in Singapore at the time, she had reached what many would consider the height of her career. But she was also experiencing severe burnout and unexplained health issues. So she made a drastic decision.

“There was this tiny little voice in me saying, ‘Maybe you should quit’,” she told FMT Lifestyle. “Everyone thought I was crazy and even my company told me to take a sabbatical instead. But I really felt that I needed a break for good.”

So she resigned, sold most of her belongings and put what remained into an 18kg backpack. Her original plan was to travel for 100 days. Instead, she spent the next five years travelling through 34 countries, often with little planning.
Despite eating out for most of her life, Loh’s travels around the world eventually drew her into the culinary world, leading to her first hybrid cookbook and travel memoir.

Titled “Taste of Letting Go”, the vegan cookbook is being brought to life through a crowdfunding campaign on Kickstarter. Launched in August 2026, it raised RM10,479 from 49 backers in its first week and officially reached its RM36,803 funding goal on Sept 12.
Now based in Brussels with her husband, Loh explained what led her to become a chef and, soon, a self-published author.
“Throughout my travels, everywhere I went, taking a culinary class was a must,” she recalled. “I learnt from everyone including Michelin-starred chefs and home cooks.”
From Kenya, Nepal and Morocco to Italy, Spain and Thailand, the techniques and recipes Loh picked up along the way were endless. Her relationship with food was changing too.
In 2018, a year into her travels, Loh met a fellow traveller who observed a raw vegan diet. The encounter inspired her to go vegan for ethical reasons.
Food soon became one of the ways Loh connected with people and places, particularly through the Couchsurfing community.

“Whenever a host had me stay with them, I would ask what their favourite meal was and then cook a vegan version for them,” she said. “Almost everyone would tell me that I should make a business out of it.”
Before long, Loh began offering private cooking and meal-preparation services to vegan communities in the cities she visited.
“When I settled down in Belgium in 2020, I started a plant-based supper club,” she shared.
SupperclubBE is Loh’s intimate monthly supper club, where she hosts eight to 12 guests at home with menus inspired by the countries she has travelled.
“I even have a regular who has never missed a supper club. Everyone kept asking me to share the recipes and those were the voices that made me think, ‘Maybe I should write a book.’”

In fact, her supper club guests voted on some of the dishes they wanted to see included in the book. “Taste of Letting Go” features 34 plant-based recipes, including a special chapter dedicated to Malaysia's banana leaf meal.
“That chapter is very special because it’s the flavours of home and the only chapter with multiple recipes. It’s also an absolute favourite among the supper club guests.”
The components include everything from rice and dal to cabbage, fried mushrooms and marinated tofu, as well as a twist on peanut potato curry.
Other recipes in the book include her take on Spain’s sardinhas assadas, traditionally grilled sardines, which she recreates using rice paper.
“Vish and chips” gets its flaky, meaty texture from marinated jackfruit, while her Hawaiian-style mac and cheese comes with vegan cheese made from scratch using sweet potatoes, mustard and cashews.
With a public retail launch planned for early 2027, Kickstarter backers will receive their copies first. The campaign remains open until Sept 18.

“My hope is that when people read the book, they think about my journey behind each recipe and perhaps take a moment to reflect on their own lives. And when they make these dishes for someone else, they can share that story too.”

b8cff1fdb7e8b0ae: Pada Hari Malaysia, kita menyaksikan satu rampasan kuasa (coup d'état) yang tidak pernah berlaku sebelum ini dan tidak berpelembagaan: ahli Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri Sembilan (exco) menerbitkan satu kenyataan bersama yang cuba mengesahkan cubaan merampas kuasa yang sumbang dan kelihatannya terancang, terhadap kedaulatan Raja Melayu.
Ini adalah pengkhianatan jentera negeri yang semakin memuncak, diketuai seorang menteri besar yang telah menjadi penderhaka kepada takhta.

Ini dilakukan walaupun Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU)—pihak berkuasa perlembagaan dan adat tertinggi di Negeri Sembilan—telah mengisytiharkan lebih awal tindakan cuba menggugat tahta Yang Dipertuan Besar adalah penderhakaan mengikut undang-undang dan adat. Sebarang proklamasi yang cuba menyingkirkan Yang Dipertuan Besar adalah batal, tidak berpelembagaan, dan tidak berasas sejak dari mula.

Nampaknya, penderhaka ini tidak mengambil masa lama mempamerkan warna sebenar mereka. Dan lihatlah bagaimana mereka memperalatkan Adat Perpatih untuk mengelak daripada kebertanggungjawaban, mewujudkan seakan perisai di mana mereka cuba berlindung daripada penguatkuasaan undang-undang.

Kebiadapan melampau individu ini sangat terserlah. Mereka baru saja mengangkat sumpah di hadapan Raja Melayu yang sama yang cuba mereka gulingkan hanya lebih sebulan lalu, dan sebahagian mereka juga menerima darjah kebesaran daripada Yang Dipertuan Besar sama tidak berapa lama dahulu.

Untuk melutut di hadapan seorang Raja Melayu bagi menerima pengiktirafan dan mengangkat sumpah jawatan, hanya untuk berpaling semula dan terlibat secara aktif dalam rampasan kuasa menggulingkan baginda, adalah kemuncak kebankrapan moral dan pengkhianatan politik.
Pelakon-pelakon subversif berkenaan beroperasi di bawah khayalan melampau portfolio pentadbiran negeri kononnya memberi hak untuk mereka memahkota atau menyingkirkan seorang Raja Melayu.

Di Negeri Sembilan, pelantikan eksekutif langsung tidak mempunyai nilai hak kuasa berhubung pewarisan takhta—satu kuasa mutlak yang berakar umbi dalam Undang-undang Tubuh Kerajaan Negeri dan tradisi suci Adat Perpatih.

Exco berfungsi sebagai badan pentadbir menguruskan portfolio negeri, menjalankan kuasa eksekutif semata-mata atas nama Yang Dipertuan Besar. Ia mempunyai sifar bidang kuasa perlembagaan untuk campur tangan dalam institusi Yang Dipertuan Besar.

Dalam krisis yang belum pernah terjadi ini, DKU tegas melaksanakan kuasa tertingginya mengecam gerakan exco sebagai rampasan kuasa tidak berpelembagaan dan satu perbuatan derhaka, mengisytiharkan sebarang cubaan menyingkirkan Yang Dipertuan Besar terbatal sama sekali.

Pengkhianatan itu paling ketara dalam sebuah entiti politik yang platform asasnya mendakwa memperjuang dan membela Raja-Raja Melayu. Sebaliknya, entiti tersebut memilih kepentingan politik, berbanding keluhuran perlembagaan.

Apabila mendalangi atau menyokong penderhakaan ini, mereka telah mendedahkan diri sebagai pengkhianat kepada perjuangan mereka sendiri, menukar kesetiaan yang suci kepada Raja Melayu demi kepentingan politik.

Rampasan kuasa terbabit adalah kempen persepsi direka teliti untuk menghasilkan kekacauan perlembagaan yang direka-reka. Dianjurkan di sebalik pintu tertutup, komplot itu bergantung pada mesej awam yang diselaraskan dan naratif berita sensasi digembar-gemburkan untuk memberi tekanan kepada jentera negeri dan memaksa warta rasmi.

Individu-individu ini tidak tiba di persimpangan dengan tangan yang bersih. Apabila kepentingan komersial peribadi, urus niaga tanah yang meragukan, dan konsesi sumber—seperti yang mengelilingi unsur nadir bumi (REE)—bergabung dengan usaha untuk meruntuhkan ketenteraman perlembagaan, ia menunjukkan sesuatu yang jauh lebih berbahaya daripada ketidakpatuhan mudah: cubaan terancang menggulingkan seorang Raja Melayu demi mengeksploitasi aset negeri di bawah lindungan kekeliruan adat yang palsu.
Di tengah-tengah pergolakan politik ini, penjawat awam Negeri Sembilan mesti terus teguh, setia kepada Raja Melayu, dan penuh komited menegakkan keluhuran Perlembagaan.

Penjawat awam terikat dengan sumpah jawatan rasmi mereka untuk menumpahkan taat setia yang sebenarnya kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar dan kedaulatan undang-undang, bukan kepada ahli politik yang cuba meruntuhkan pihak berkuasa diraja demi cita-cita peribadi. Untuk goyah atau tunduk kepada tekanan politik adalah satu pengkhianatan kepada kepercayaan awam dan tunggak asas pentadbiran negeri.
Gugat Raja Melayu penderhakaan tertinggi

Dari sudut sejarah, di bawah Adat Perpatih, derhaka tidak pernah dianggap ringan. Pepatah adat 'terbuang ke rimba, dihanyutkan ke laut' mentakrifkan keterukannya—pesalah menghadapi penarikan gelaran, pemulauan total, dan dibuang negeri. Tradisi tidak pernah bertolak ansur dengan mereka yang memperalatkan adat terhadap kedaulatan Raja Melayu.

Di luar adat, hujah perundangannya sangat jelas tanpa kekaburan. Perlindungan Raja-Raja Melayu termaktub dalam Perlembagaan Persekutuan di bawah Perkara 71 dan 181(1). Di bawah Seksyen 121 dan 121A Kanun Keseksaan, kesalahan menggugat kedaulatan seorang Raja membawa hukuman berkanun yang berat, termasuk penjara seumur hidup. Digabungkan dengan Akta Hasutan, menggugat seorang Raja Melayu adalah penderhakaan tertinggi di sisi undang-undang persekutuan.

Tambahan pula, daulat itu benar. Lebih kuat oportunis politik berkonspirasi terhadap seorang Raja Melayu yang sah berdarah Raja tulen, lebih kuat tindak balas yang membalas kembali. Kuasa kerohanian dan legitimasi perlembagaan bukanlah alat politik untuk dipermainkan.

Menambahkan lagi kejelasan undang-undang, Jabatan Peguam Negara (AGC) telah mengesahkan secara rasmi bahawa exco dan menteri besar tidak mempunyai sebarang kuasa undang-undang untuk menyingkirkan Yang Dipertuan Besar secara unilateral, serta mengisytiharkan tindakan mereka terbatal sepenuhnya dan tidak berperlembagaan.
Pendirian berwibawa itu memadamkan sebarang sisa legitimasi yang cuba direka konspirator, sekali gus menggariskan jawatan pentadbiran tidak memberi kuasa meruntuhkan kedaulatan undang-undang.

Agensi penguatkuasaan undang-undang persekutuan, AGC, dan institusi negeri mesti bertanya pada diri sendiri: berapa lama lagi penderhakaan yang terang-terangan ini akan dibiarkan tanpa penguatkuasaan undang-undang?

Negeri Sembilan dibina di atas undang-undang, tradisi, dan ketenteraman perlembagaan. Ia tidak boleh diserahkan kepada ahli politik yang cuba bermain sebagai pentabal raja. Penderhakaan telah dinamakan, pelaku telah didedahkan, dan keadilan mesti ditegakkan tanpa rasa takut atau pilih kasih ketika di puncak krisis ini.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
d912a7b366944a42: WASHINGTON: US lawmakers from both parties attacked President Donald Trump's mass deportation drive Thursday, with a member of his own party warning that Hispanic voters who helped return him to the White House now "feel betrayed".

"Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Republican congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida said in a campaign video released weeks before November's midterm elections.

Salazar, whose Miami-area district is overwhelmingly Hispanic, said half of roughly 50,000 people detained in July had no criminal record, and she urged Trump to reconsider advice he was receiving on immigration.
"The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today," she said.
"I'm not talking about giving them amnesty. I'm talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land."

The unusually direct rebuke from a Republican comes as the party controlling Congress and the White House faces growing concern that aggressive immigration enforcement could erode gains the president made among Latino voters in 2024.
Trump endorsed Salazar earlier this year, although the American former television journalist, who has Cuban heritage, has long advocated legal status for some undocumented immigrants.
Her intervention came hours before Democrats in the Congressional Hispanic Caucus accused the administration of inflicting both a human and economic toll through mass deportations.

At a Capitol Hill news conference with immigration advocacy group America's Voice, lawmakers blamed US Immigration and Customs Enforcement for rising costs associated with labour shortages – assailing what they called the "ICE tax".

"ICE is an affordability issue. Everyone in this country is paying the ICE tax," caucus chairman Adriano Espaillat said, arguing that removing workers was pushing up the costs of food, construction and health care.
House Democrat Joaquin Castro of Texas said immigration raids were removing workers from industries including agriculture, construction and restaurants.
"ICE is killing the American economy," Castro said, pointing to businesses struggling to find workers and consumers paying higher prices.
California Democrat Gil Cisneros said labour shortages in his state had caused more than US$3 billion in crop losses and driven produce prices higher.
Trump campaigned on carrying out the largest deportation operation in US history and has sharply expanded arrests since returning to office.
But Salazar's warning highlighted the political tension for Republicans representing large Hispanic communities as enforcement moves beyond immigrants accused of serious crimes.
"Be careful what your advisors are telling you about immigration policy," she told Trump.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
73daee235465a91d: FRANKFURT: Jurgen Klopp said on Thursday that Germany's football team can help ensure "national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people" after a recent far-right AfD election victory.

In a Frankfurt press conference announcing his first squad as Germany manager, the former Liverpool coach referenced a recent state election landslide win by the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany party.
The AfD won almost 44 percent of the vote in the former East German state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6 and expects strong results in elections Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Klopp took over the Germany job in July after the four-time World Cup winners suffered a third straight early elimination at the tournament.
The 59-year-old has often spoke out about social issues during his time as manager of Liverpool, Borussia Dortmund and Mainz.
While not mentioning the AfD by name, Klopp advocated for adopting "positive patriotism", while saying: "I don't want to entrust national pride to the wrong people.
"A crazy amount of things have happened not that long ago. There was a vote which some people probably found OK, but others would have thought 'good heavens, what's going on here?'"
"From the perspective of someone in sport, I'd like to reclaim the flag for myself and for us. When we wave it, I don't want that someone thinks 'what's going on with you?'
"I want that they think you're happy and you understand how lucky you are to be born in this wonderful country or to have moved here and live here."
Topics involving patriotism and nationalism are often sensitive in Germany, a country still at pains to atone for its dark history of Nazi rule, World War II and the Holocaust.
Speaking of national pride, Klopp said he was "not even sure if one can – or is allowed to – use that term anymore without it being misunderstood."
"I can be proud of being German and still be open, diverse, kind and friendly."
The coach said it was more important that the country had enough doctors and caregivers, but said football can "foster a sense of community here, allowing us to truly feel the power of sport."
On Thursday, Klopp took the unusual step of naming a huge 44-man squad for four upcoming Nations League matches, despite matchday lists being restricted to 23 players.
"It's very unusual that you've got four games in two weeks with the national team," Klopp said.
"I want to get to know as many players as possible in that time."
Klopp won the Champions League and Premier League during a trophy-laden nine-year stint at Liverpool.--AFP

c95a59b4416480eb: WASHINGTON: US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh delivered the interest rate hike this week that many economists think surging inflation required, defying President Donald Trump – but questions about the central bank chief's credibility linger.
The Fed on Wednesday raised rates in the world's largest economy by 25 basis points to between 3.75% and 4%, with policymakers signalling at least one more rate hike before year-end.

Trump has launched an unprecedented assault on the Fed's independence to set monetary policy since taking office, initiating a criminal probe into Warsh's predecessor and attempting to fire another Fed governor in his quest for lower rates to spur economic activity.
He frequently insulted and berated former chair Jerome Powell but delivered a muted – if still extraordinary – response to Warsh's announcement of the rate hike.

Trump told reporters he spoke with Warsh before the Fed's meeting, telling him to "do what you want" and ascribing the decision to raise rates – which the Fed chair voted for and stood by – to a "hostile board".
Asked by a reporter if he had spoken to the president, Warsh was tight-lipped. And queried on the Fed's independence, he again offered a tepid defence.

"Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane. Independence is a two-way street," he said, responding to a question about Trump's threat to cut trade ties with some countries if the Fed raised rates.
"We let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane, too," Warsh said.
For Pao-Lin Tien, economics professor at George Washington University, Trump's version of his conversation with Warsh will fuel the scepticism of those who question the latter's independence.
"That kind of meddling really makes people question a little bit whether the Fed chair is really completely independent," she said. "Personally, I'm not very convinced."
'Not a reliable narrator'

For others, however, Warsh has been put in a difficult spot. With inflation surging to three-year highs amid the Iran war, and an aggressive president who has made it clear he will channel his anger at friends and foes alike if he does not get what he wants.
David Wessel, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, thought Warsh managed the situation well.

"He got a unanimous vote from the FOMC to raise interest rates, and, apparently based on a conversation between the two men, the president doesn't seem to blame Warsh personally for the rate hike," he said, referring to the Fed's interest-rate setting committee.
Still, the president's assertion that he gave Warsh permission to vote for the hike was "very Trump-like", he added.

"We don't know what was really said in that conversation. Warsh isn't talking and Trump isn't a reliable narrator," said Wessel. "I doubt he asked Trump for permission, but maybe Trump believes he gave it."
'Steel in his spine'
What is clear to many economists is that a rate hike was needed.
Inflation has been above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for more than five years, with US households and businesses battered by high prices since the pandemic.
Inflation had been on a downward trajectory, but prices have surged in the wake of Trump's war on Iran, his signature tariff policies and the ongoing AI boom.
Since taking office in May, Warsh has made it clear he was focused on the high prices.
"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," he told reporters on Wednesday.
The White House insists that any inflation is due to the previous administration, with Trump advisor Kevin Hassett saying earlier this week that there was no need for a rate hike to tackle it.
Warsh, however, had a different view, saying that inflation data over the summer did not suggest that price rises were transitory.
For Tien, the Fed's decision to raise rates may have defied Trump's demands, but it does not necessarily mean much for its independence.
"Inflation has been so high for so long that it will be very hard to make an argument to not raise rates," she said.
Many in financial markets, however, cheered Wednesday's decision as establishing Warsh's credibility in going against the White House's wishes.
"Warsh has shown that he has steel in his spine by increasing interest rates seven weeks before the midterm elections," wrote economist Michael Strain in the Financial Times.

b9318b1f522a1971: WASHINGTON: Meta on Thursday moved to remove AI-generated videos targeting two women, including a British politician, after the tech giant's Oversight Board blasted its "fundamentally inadequate" safeguards against proliferating deepfakes.

The Oversight Board, the quasi-independent body the company funds to review its moderation decisions, earlier Thursday demanded that Meta remove the fabricated videos from its platforms, saying the cases undermined its own policies on hate speech, misinformation and harassment.

The first AI-generated video depicted a Labour Party councillor in Scotland making incendiary comments about refugees. There was no public record of the politician making the comment, and the video showed telltale signs of fabrication, including audio that was not synchronised to her facial movements.

The second fabricated video targeted a Muslim woman campaigner in Europe and sought to discredit her role as a health advocate by falsely depicting her consuming junk food while giving advice about mindful eating and engaging in absurd exercises.
The board said Meta's policies are "consistently and fundamentally inadequate" to address the growing flood of AI-generated content on its platforms, which include Facebook and Instagram.

"From politicians to private citizens, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly being used to harass and silence women from engaging in public discourse," Oversight Board co-chair Pamela San Martin said in a statement.
"These cases demonstrate a broader, troubling pattern in which women who engage publicly on issues are disproportionately subjected to harassment and misinformation."
The Oversight Board's decisions on individual cases are binding on Meta, but its broader policy recommendations are not.
Meta said it welcomed the board's decision in both cases and will comply within seven days.

"Meta and other social media platforms need more robust policies to address the proliferation of deepfakes, including a much stronger approach to labelling deceptive content, stricter penalties for repeat offenders, and the removal of deepfakes harassing private individuals," said San Martin.
Last week, the board urged Meta not to replace professional fact-checking with Community Notes, a crowdsourced model for debunking falsehoods popularised by billionaire Elon Musk's platform X.
The plea came after Meta said it had begun testing Community Notes in 16 Spanish-speaking countries in Latin America, in a step toward replacing its fact-checking programme.
AFP currently works in 26 languages with Meta's global fact-checking programme, including in Latin America.

a3bd6686ad2d854b: BERLIN: Germany coach Juergen Klopp said on Thursday that he wanted to reclaim expressions of national pride from the "wrong people," in remarks widely seen as a rebuke to the far right after the Alternative for Germany (AfD) won an election this month.

Speaking at a press conference to unveil a 44-man split squad for upcoming Nations League matches, Klopp said Germans should feel able to express pride in their country without being associated with extremism.
"I don't want to leave national pride to the wrong people," said Klopp, one of the country's most prominent public figures.
Without mentioning the AfD by name, he added that he would like to "reclaim the flag."
"I want it so that when someone waves it, no one thinks: 'What is wrong with you?'," said Klopp.
"Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country," he said.

The AfD trounced mainstream parties to win an election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sept 6, and could form the first far-right government at state level in postwar Germany there. It could also top the polls in another state election this weekend.

"There have been an incredible number of things happening recently: an election took place which some people probably thought was fine, whilst many others thought, ‘Good heavens, what on earth is going on?'," Klopp said.
An AfD spokesperson said the party would issue a statement later on Thursday.

German finance minister and vice chancellor Lars Klingbeil said he shared Klopp's view, saying the German flag - with its three horizontal stripes in black, red and gold - was not a symbol of exclusion or arrogance.
"People can be proud of this country, regardless of whether they were born here, have immigrated here, or their family has lived here for generations," he told Reuters.
"National pride and an open-minded attitude towards the world are not mutually exclusive."

Wearing a cap with an Adidas logo in the colours of the German flag, Klopp acknowledged the sensitivity of patriotism in a country that has long viewed overt displays of national pride through the prism of its Nazi past.
The former Liverpool manager, who begins his tenure against the Netherlands on Sept 24, said he preferred the term "positive patriotism" to "national pride", which he feared could be misunderstood.
"Can you be proud to be German and still be open, diverse, nice and friendly - can you still show compassion?" Klopp said.
The secretary general of chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats, Franziska Hoppermann, welcomed Klopp's call to not leave Germany's symbols to the extremists.
"We all should, and are allowed to, wear our national colours with pride and confidence as symbols of our freedom," she told Reuters.

At 102, Saimah Sajiman has no complicated formula for staying healthy.
She simply sticks to the routines she has followed for decades, including eating simple food and keeping regular mealtimes.

Fondly known as Tok Saimah, the centenarian from Kampung Rahmat, Sri Lalang, believes that maintaining a healthy diet, particularly choosing boiled food over fried or oily dishes, is among the practices that have helped her stay healthy.

"It is not that I do not eat fried food, but I prefer boiled food such as 'sayur bening' (clear vegetable soup), 'ikan pais' (steamed fish with spices) and traditional village 'ulam' (vegetable salads)," she said at her home.
Born in 1924, Tok Saimah, who has more than 20 grandchildren and 50 great-grandchildren, said she would have her breakfast, lunch and dinner at almost the same time every day.
"For breakfast, I will have something light to line the stomach, usually between 8am and 9am. Lunch is before the zohor prayer and dinner is before the isyak prayer," she said.
Her daughter, Fatimah Surip, 78, said she was grateful that her mother remained in good health and was able to stand while performing her prayers.

"My mother does not suffer from any chronic diseases, just a slight hearing problem. If you want to converse, you have to speak a little louder. She also prefers using a wheelchair to move from one place to another," she said.
Tok Saimah recently gained attention on social media after receiving a visit from Her Majesty Raja Zarith Sofiah, Queen of Malaysia, last Sunday.

Fatimah said her mother's age and experiences of living through several eras, including the Japanese occupation, British colonial rule and the communist terrorist threat, were among the topics that drew Her Majesty's attention during the visit.

a27c34507684f5c0: In response to a new European Union law, AI platforms are implementing new schemes for watermarking the content they generate. Anthropic recently disclosed its future Claude models will use SynthID-Text, an approach Google created and released as open source. It uses a secret key that subtly changes the process a model uses for choosing the next word in a sentence. Whereas a top next word choice might be “cloudy,” the key might change it to “overcast.” Anyone who knows the key can determine if it was generated by the platform using it.

New research shows that SynthID-Text can change not just word selection but also the tools a model invokes and the chances it will adhere to or disregard safety guardrails it has been trained to follow. The threat can become greater in the face of an adversarial prompt, in which an attacker attempts to cause a model to carry out a harmful action, such as revealing a password or other sensitive information. Instructions that normally wouldn’t be followed will, in some cases, be performed once the watermarking is deployed. The finding underscores the need for developers to thoroughly test how their LLMs and agents behave when watermarking is in place.

“As compared to the same models without watermarking, it is definitely going to change their behavior, especially when we place it under adversarial conditions, or we make these models call tools when they’re powering an agent,” Andrea Siposova, an AI security researcher at Lasso Security, told Ars. “Watermarking is made to not be perceptible to a reader, but we know that when we are changing anything about what the model is generating, it is going to cause some tradeoffs, it’s going to show up somewhere.”

bc87ff8a33aff370: China’s Salt Typhoon gang has developed a new backdoor and dropped it in networks belonging to high-profile organizations in several countries across Central and South America since at least August 2025, according to researchers. The PRC-backed espionage crew shifted its focus to Latin America a month prior, and from mid-2025 into 2026, the vast majority - 90 percent - of Salt Typhoon’s targets were located in that region, ESET, which tracks the group as FamousSparrow, said in a Thursday report. Salt Typhoon is the cyber-spy gang that hacked telecommunications and government agencies to gain stealthy, long-term access to victim organizations going back as far as 2019. These hacks, however, weren’t discovered until late 2023. In August 2025, ESET’s malware hunters found the group’s new backdoor, called SparroWocky, deployed against government agencies in Argentina, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, Peru, Puerto Rico, and Venezuela. While targeting entities in these countries “represents a rare occurrence among the China-aligned APT groups,” ESET believes the focus likely reflects China’s reaction to recent US President Donald Trump’s initiatives in the region, malware researchers Alexandre Côté Cyr and Romain Dumont said. “Donald Trump’s second presidential term has brought about an aggressive reaffirmation of US interests in Latin America, which threatens various long-term investments that China has cultivated throughout the continent in the last decade, in domains such as energy, mining, and telecommunications,” they wrote. “We suspect that FamousSparrow’s activities are intended to help China better monitor and anticipate the reaction of local governments to current US pressures.” SparroWocky is a modular C++ backdoor that appeared soon after the Beijing snoops started focusing on Latin America. The new backdoor integrates open source tools and uses techniques designed to evade antivirus and other security software. The name comes from Lewis Carroll’s Jabberwocky poem - the researchers found the first stanza in several collected samples. (’Twas brillig, and the slithy toves/Did gyre and gimble in the wabe:/All mimsy were the borogoves,/And the mome raths outgrabe.) ESET based its analysis on a malware sample compiled on November 17, and said it contained the following open source projects: Mbed TLS, a C library it uses to establish a secure communication channel with its command-and-control (C2) server. MinHook, a Windows API hooking library that hides the start address of newly created threads from security products. COFF Loader (or a similar project) to enable dynamic loading and execution of in-memory plugins in the form of COFF objects. Plus, the backdoor incorporates a variant of the SilentMoonwalk technique to spoof the call stacks originating from MinHook routines, and thus escape the watchful eyes of monitoring tools, along with a custom API-hashing algorithm to dynamically resolve Windows API functions. The gang deploys the backdoor in its usual way: a trident loader scheme consisting of a legitimate executable, a malicious DLL, and a file containing the encrypted malware. The loader resides in the malicious DLL and executes via DLL side-loading. After establishing communication with its C2 server, the backdoor starts receiving commands handled by a custom class named WinHandler (derived from a ServerHandler custom class), according to the runtime type information in the malware. The nearly 30 commands include scooping up system details and sending them to the C2, starting and/or terminating a new session and removing persistence, stealing and deleting files, taking periodic screenshots, collecting session IDs and usernames of enumerated remote sessions on the system via WTSEnumerateSessionsW, and spawning new SparrowWocky instances. It uses TLS encryption to communicate with its C2 servers, connecting directly to their IP addresses, generally on port 443, although ESET also spotted the malware using port 8080 in some cases. The malware researchers also published a full indicators-of-compromise list and samples in ESET’s GitHub repository, so give those a read, too. ®

3af20cbf02359405: There's no need to actually read a whole research paper when you can ask a bot to explain it to you. Scientific papers can transform into AI agents that, according to the Stanford team behind the project, should speed up the dissemination of new scientific discoveries. Paper2Agent, the team's new framework described in a paper published in Nature on Wednesday, converts scientific papers and their associated research outputs into agents that can discuss a paper’s findings, reproduce analyses and results, apply its methods to new data, and even collaborate with other paper agents on new research problems. “Papers have been static documents for centuries,” James Zou, a Stanford computer scientist and biomedical data science professor and one of the paper’s authors, said in a LinkedIn post announcing P2A’s publication. “Paper2Agent turns them into active AI agents that can answer questions, apply their methods, and collaborate with other papers to make new discoveries.” Giving a large language model access to a scientific paper is unpredictable, Zou added. What his team wanted was an agent that could act as a “virtual author” that had hands-on experience with a paper’s work, not just reading it and attempting to understand it. What that means in practice, as explained in the paper, is a workflow that uses a paper and its associated data, repository, and codebase to create a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing the research's tools, resources, and workflows. An LLM agent can then connect to the server and use natural-language requests to autonomously run demonstrations, reproduce analyses, apply a paper's methods to new data, and the like. “Paper2Agent agentifies the full research outputs, including manuscripts, supplementary materials, code, datasets, executable examples and analysis workflows,” the researchers explained in their writeup. According to the paper, the MCP server itself can be hosted remotely, but Zou explained to The Register in an email that it can also be run locally to protect sensitive information, though such info will still be sent to whichever LLM backend P2A is connected to. “If the user has sensitive data (e.g. protected health information) that they don't want to send to an LLM then they should exclude that data from P2A,” Zou told us, adding that P2A should be compatible with any AI coding agent, but that not all have been tested. AI hallucinations are an obvious concern, and the paper notes that researchers should always evaluate anything P2A presents to be sure it’s correct. “We … view Paper2Agent as a tool for augmenting scientific discovery and improving access, reproducibility and reuse of papers, rather than as an autonomous or authoritative source of scientific conclusions,” the paper notes. That said, P2A still does its best to prevent such errors from cropping up. The paper explains that each tool used by a paper agent is validated against the paper’s results and figures and “locked to ensure reproducibility.” This decreases hallucination risk and minimizes randomness, but still - best to double-check its work. Tests to see how well P2A scales appear to have gone well, with the researchers evaluating it across 136 papers in three groups, including 100 computational-biology papers. Of those 100 papers, 74 were successfully turned into agents, with the researchers attributing failures largely to incomplete codebases, missing documentation, or unresolvable environment configurations. Still, it’s a massive leap in what could be possible when it comes to getting new scientific discoveries into the hands of more researchers. P2A is open source, and is available on GitHub for those who want to take a stab at it. There’s also a live version online that can explain the P2A paper in more detail and reproduce its results, and Zou tells us it can also ingest other papers to see how it works on their projects. Zou explained to us that he hopes the open source community will help improve P2A, but notes that his team isn’t done with it either. Next up, they hope to create an online platform for paper agents to collaborate and discuss various “agentified” scientific discoveries. Let’s just hope those boffin bots behave a bit better than their counterparts. ®

Dray Agha, senior manager of security operations at Huntress, explained that Metabase connects to customers' databases, so the information exposed in an attack depends on the access each customer granted it. "A company linking Metabase to a general analytics database will only expose harmless user metrics," he said. "A company that connects it directly to their core transactional database risks exposing highly sensitive financial records and credentials." Agha said that if the exposed passwords and financial details were stored in readable form, that would point to inadequate data protection practices. "Sensitive financial details should also be encrypted or tokenized when held in a database. Keeping this information readable creates a massive risk if a connected reporting tool is ever compromised." The Register understands that City Relay sent the emails to current landlords and former users of its services. One source claimed City Relay learned of the intrusion on September 8 and notified affected customers on September 14. "As property access and key-storage information was potentially included, we immediately took precautionary action to update the relevant access and key-storage codes," the emails stated. "This work has now been completed. The previously exposed codes can no longer be used and we have no evidence of any unauthorised property access arising from the incident." Beyond the immediate physical security risks, City Relay urged customers to check their bank accounts for suspicious transactions, watch for phishing and other scams, and change any reused passwords on other accounts. The company told us it had found no evidence that the exposed data had been misused. It is continuing to investigate alongside cybersecurity specialists and "the relevant authorities" to establish the attack's full scope. City Relay's website says it has hundreds of "partners" – landlords who outsource management of their property portfolios – and that it manages, or has managed, thousands of London properties. The company has not said how many customers were affected in London or Paris, where it also operates. The Register asked City Relay for more information. City Relay did not identify the vulnerability used in the attack. Metabase disclosed a zero-day SQL injection flaw on August 6, saying attackers compromised fewer than 3 percent of its customers before fixes were automatically deployed, but it has not confirmed that the City Relay incident was part of that campaign. Known victims included laptop maker Framework and workflow automation platform n8n. ®

cd6dc46133d3f1bd: From Clement Stanley
The next Melaka state election is due within the next five months but the rival parties have already begun sounding the war drums. And none louder than Umno.

It reached a crescendo at the recent Umno general assembly, where party president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi and some of their leaders laid bare their intention to take over the reins of the federal government with the help of PAS.
Hence, the repeated call by Zahid and Umno for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim to dissolve Parliament before the five-year term of the Madani government ends.

But Anwar can ignore such calls. He has, after all, another 15 months to go. Anything can happen in that time. Nothing is certain even though Umno and PAS have started counting their chickens before they are hatched.

The manner in which Umno dared the prime minister to remove its members from the Cabinet at its recent general assembly underscored, or perhaps reiterated, one thing: the arrogance that contributed to their ouster in 2018 was never truly exorcised.
And all it took was - from an outsider’s point of view at least - two state elections to abandon calls for the party to heed lessons from its worst electoral outing.
The wins in Johor and Negeri Sembilan have apparently returned the “we-are-untouchable” swagger Umno had for the longest time prior to 2018.
Electoral wins do boost one’s confidence, but there is a fine line between cockiness and delusion.
However, there is one way to test this theory, and it comes from Umno Youth chief Dr Akmal Saleh.
Akmal challenged Pakatan Harapan to go solo and contest all 28 seats up for grabs in the next Melaka state election, telling them to forget working with Barisan Nasional.
But instead of telling PH to go solo, perhaps BN, led by Umno, should do the same.
Forget about working with PAS.
BN won handsomely in Johor and Negeri Sembilan in part due to the tacit or explicit support of PAS in those two states.
Does BN know how much of an impact vote transference played a part in these victories? Or is Umno’s leadership trying to kid itself?
The proof is in the pudding and maybe BN should put their money where its mouth is and just go solo at the Melaka polls.
On another note, Umno’s arrogance should also serve as a red flag for PAS.
After winning just one state election on an understanding with PAS, Umno wants PAS to prove its loyalty to “Malay unity” by holding an election in Terengganu.
What will happen if Umno wins more seats with PAS's help in the future? What would Umno demand then? Subservience and total submission?
Maybe this is a good reason for PAS to paraphrase Akmal by telling BN to “forget about working with PAS. Go ahead and contest all 28 seats”.
But would Umno be brave enough to do just that despite the chest thumping at their general assembly? I doubt it. They would not have the guts to do that.
Clement Stanley is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
